Moreover, it allows for the construction of a straightforward and manageable series form of these expressions. Notably, the relevance of these relations extends beyond QCD expressions to other related topological series in field theory.

This research focuses on chordal power graphs associated with finite groups. We demonstrate in this work that the chordal power graphs are present in finite groups of the type $G=\langle x,y \rangle \times G_1$, where $G_1$ is either cyclic or a direct product of two cyclic groups. We further discover that the chordal power graph is unique to these specific types of groups.

This research introduces an innovative training method, optimal condition training, to enhance SC TC-RNN performance in single-channel target source separation tasks. By capitalizing on the unique properties of normalizing single-channel inputs, the network can be effectively learned under ideal conditions without any prior knowledge. Experimental results confirm that using the OCT method in conjunction with a single-channel deep convolutional recurrent network (DCRNN) yields significantly improved performance over the standard supervised learning approach.

This research explores the quantum Fisher information of incoherent states within the context of symmetric non-Hermitian models, yielding exact expressions for this quantity in both two-state and three-state scenarios. It is discovered that the quantum Fisher information for such states is directly proportional to the square of the real part of a specific matrix element, enabling a detailed comparison of monopartite quantum systems derived from non-Hermitian systems versus their Hermitian counterparts in the classical limit.

Our research examined the behavior of the soft X-ray transition in GRS 1749-28 (H 1743-322) from hard to soft state. We discovered that the amplitude of the QPOs is significantly reduced during the transition phase, with the highest amplitude QPOs disappearing before the lowest frequency QPOs appear. This pattern is similar to patterns seen in other transients. We found that the amplitude of QPOs is higher in the decay phase than in the rise phase, with the exception of high frequency QPOs which are more pronounced in the rise phase. We suggest that the QPO source responsible for the highest amplitude QPOs is blocked by an increase in the accretion disk corona's density. We propose that the QPO source responsible for the lowest frequency QPOs is uncovered as the corona's density decreases, leading to an increase in the strength of the lowest frequency QPOs during the soft state transition.

This study introduces a set of tools and methods for creating question answering systems, focusing specifically on Romanian language. We examine the process of transforming an existing information retrieval system into one capable of performing question answering by utilizing a large news corpus. We develop an open-source, rule-based system for extracting knowledge and introduce our own dataset containing approximately 3.5 million questions and answers, annotated following the SQuAD format, for the Romanian language. We assess the performance of question answering systems, both with and without the addition of external knowledge sources, and demonstrate that our systems can achieve results comparable to those for English and other languages with larger available resources, achieving 23.75% and 31.95% scores respectively for the former and the latter.

The distribution of missing baryons, primarily in the form of warm and hot
intergalactic gas, is linked to the cosmic web at a redshift of 0.03. By
combining data from the \emph{Sloan Digital Sky Survey} and the \emph{Hubble
Supernova Legacy Survey}, we investigate the correlation between the mass of
hot gas and the properties of the cosmic web, as defined by the Discrete
Galaxy Field. We find a significant association between the mass of hot gas and
various cosmic web parameters, with a notable effect observed when considering
the effects of redshift. We also discover that the distribution of hot gas is
primarily influenced by the underlying matter distribution, rather than the
cosmic web structure itself. By simulating the distribution of hot gas using a
simple model, we are able to replicate the observed correlation with the
cosmic web. Our results have implications for our understanding of the
distribution of baryons in the universe and the processes governing the
intergalactic medium.

We have developed a new algorithm to approximate the treewidth of graphs, which can be executed in O((2k-1) * (log k)^k) time for a given integer k representing the desired treewidth, and it operates in O((k-1)(log k)^k) space. This is an improvement upon existing O((k log k)^k) time and O((k^3 (log k)^k) space bounds from prior research. This advancement is a result of our innovative use of multivariate analysis over tree decomposition, facilitated by a novel combination of multivariate recurrence and bucket data structures that support operations such as addition, subtraction, and minimum detection in near-constant time.

A comprehensive analysis of a sample of 240 post-starburst galaxies at redshifts between 0.2 and 1.6, based on data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, has been conducted. This analysis aimed to identify and classify transient events, specifically Type Ia supernovae and Tidal Disruption Events, both of which are related to the remnants of recent starburst activity. Utilizing a combination of photometric redshifts and machine learning techniques, the researchers distinguished between Type Ia supernovae and Tidal Disruption Events, with photometric redshifts used as an initial filter. This reduced the number of candidates to 22, which were then further analyzed using a machine learning algorithm. This approach resulted in a 50% higher detection rate of Tidal Disruption Events, specifically 8 events, compared to the use of a simple Bayesian approach, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.3 to -0.1 in the k-correction of M_u. This analysis suggests that the rates of Type Ia supernovae and Tidal Disruption Events are comparable, with the former occurring at a rate of 1.1 per 100,000 years and the latter at a rate of 0.9 per 100,000 years. This finding has implications for the study of the rate of Tidal Disruption Events, indicating that they are more common than previously estimated.

In 5G NR systems, the innovative resource block scheduling approach has been adopted, which presents a complex optimization problem to be resolved. In this paper, we introduce a novel policy-based scheduling method, which leverages actor-critic learning-based techniques to address this problem. By modeling the system dynamics as a Markov decision process, we develop a policy that maximizes the expected system utility. Actor-critic method's convergence ensures that the policy converges towards an optimal solution. Simulation results demonstrate that the actor-critic learning-based scheduler outperforms traditional scheduling techniques in terms of system utility. Furthermore, the results show that the actor-critic method achieves significant gains of 4.8% and 4.5% in terms of system utility compared to max-min resource block scheduling and the max sum utility based scheduling respectively.

In recent years, word-level quality estimation has gained significant attention 
due to the shift from sentence-based to document-level text. However, a major 
drawback of using word-level QE is that it fails to preserve the original 
functionality of sentence-level QE, which is an essential tool for teachers 
in language education. To address this issue, this study proposes a refined 
word-level QE model that not only evaluates sentence-level quality but also 
provides insights into word-level quality. To this end, a novel dataset has 
been created by adding a word-level label to an existing dataset, and 
experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new model compared 
to a standard word-level QE model.

A new Kerr-de Sitter black hole solution is developed from an asymptotically flat space-time by a non-linear transformation, and its properties are further studied by incorporating accretion flows. By analyzing the shadow cast by this new black hole, we observe notable differences from M\`oszkes' shadow, with the most striking feature being an asymmetrical shape. Accretion flows on this new black hole reveal features distinct from conventional thin accretion disks, both in terms of photon geodesic trajectories and brightness patterns.

We introduce a novel flux-conservative formulation of one-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics in Spherical Coordinates, building upon an existing algorithm by Moll et al. Our formulation adheres to the conservative update equation and ensures entropy satisfaction, distinguishing it from previous relativistic numerical algorithms that frequently suffer from entropy violation and excessive damping. To validate its effectiveness, we conduct a thorough analysis by applying our flux-conservative algorithm to a set of benchmark tests covering shock waves, neutron star crashes, and black hole mergers, using both ideal and viscous fluid models and a fully general relativistic spacetime context. Our results show that the new algorithm significantly outperforms previous relativistic hydro codes in terms of accuracy and shock capturing.

The LHCb experiment discovered four previously unknown resonances of the $D_{s0}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s1}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s0}^*(2860)^0$ and $D_{s1}^*(2865)^0$ states through the analysis of decay processes involving the $D^* K^0_{\rm S}$. The observed resonances are classified as $D_{s0}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s1}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s0}^*(2860)^0$ and $D_{s1}^*(2865)^0$. A comprehensive theoretical model was developed to explain these resonances. The model incorporates the interplay of excitation mechanisms including both creation through the $c\bar{c}$ and $b\bar{b}$ states and the strong decay processes involving the $c\bar{u}$ and $c\bar{s}$ transitions. The model's success in reproducing the observed resonances and their properties is notable. The model's predictions for the properties of the $D_{s0}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s1}^*(2595)^0$, $D_{s0}^*(2860)^0$ and $D_{s1}^*(2865)^0$ states are provided. The model's

We propose novel methods for estimating the fractal dimensions of functions defined on the Sierpi\'nski Gasket using its sample entropy and correlation dimension. Furthermore, these measures are used to analyze the dimension of the graph obtained from a distance-preserving map. A function to determine if a given graph is related to the graph of a distance-preserving map is put forth. Additionally, a procedure is developed for calculating the fractal dimension of the graph obtained from a composition of distance-preserving maps.

To generate and improve photo captions, we have a question generation model that produces direct questions based on the images, but it tends to produce captions that are irrelevant or grammatically incorrect. This model can be transformed into a captioning model by fine-tuning it with image-caption pairs, a method that works well when the model is able to produce questions relevant to the images. To rectify this, we propose a method to provide guidance to the question generation model, which is based on the idea of comparing generated questions to the free descriptions provided with the images. By fine-tuning the model with paired pairs that match relevant questions with their corresponding captions, we observe significant improvements in the quality of the generated questions, with a notable increase in the accuracy and grammatical correctness of the produced captions.

The dark matter halo's inner density profile is a crucial aspect of its structure. In dwarf galaxies, the cusp of the dark matter profile has been observed to be less steep, and in some cases, a core may even be present. A recent study has shown that dwarf galaxies located in halos with core regions can have a dark matter core size that depends on the core radius of their parent halo. This study aims to investigate how the core radius of a dark matter halo is affected by the presence of a baryonic core in the dwarf galaxy. To do so, we have simulated a dwarf galaxy located in a host halo with a core, and found that the baryonic core influences the dark matter distribution in the inner regions of the halo. Our results show that the size of the dark matter core in the halo is reduced when the baryonic core is located within a certain distance of the dwarf galaxy. This effect is due to the baryonic core's gravitational influence, and we find that the size of the dark matter core in the halo is reduced by approximately 10% for baryonic core distances of less than 50 kpc. Our study suggests that the presence of a baryonic core in dwarf galaxies can have a significant impact on the dark matter distribution in the halo, and we propose that this effect should be taken into account when studying the properties of dwarf galaxies.

In recent years, the development of techniques for resolving and optimizing Boolean satisfiability has accelerated, with the recent focus on efficient methods for eliminating variables being a significant example. This research focuses on a specific method of variable elimination, namely, the technique of eliminating a single literal from a given Boolean formula. By building on previous studies, the authors have created a more efficient implementation of a specific method called quasipure literal elimination and compared its performance to another method called pure literal elimination. Experimental results conducted on a broad range of Boolean satisfiability problems indicate that the new quasipure literal elimination approach often outperforms the traditional method, particularly when the remaining Boolean formula still contains multiple variable interactions.

We establish a general theorem concerning evolutionary game theory, which states that any two-player game with a substantial number of possible strategies for both players will have at least one stable state for both players, assuming their behavior follows an established model. This finding mirrors a well-known theorem in traditional game theory, known as the Folk Theorem, except in scenarios where the rules or limitations of the game impose restrictions. Our proof, which builds upon an existing method, relies on simplifying the game into a more manageable version and then demonstrating that this simplified form always has a stable state for both players, except in scenarios where the game is tied to a zero-sum outcome. This simplified version of the theorem is then used to prove the broader theorem, which applies to a more general model of evolutionary game theory, using a method known as backward induction. This finding has significant implications for understanding evolutionary game theory, as it provides a clear pathway for determining whether a particular outcome, or state, is stable for both players in a given game, except in scenarios where the game is tied to a zero-sum outcome.

This study introduces a new and efficient multivariate regression tree algorithm, enhancing the conventional CART method by producing point estimates for continuous outcomes and their corresponding covariance matrices, based on a Gaussian distribution assumption. The point estimates are obtained by taking the mean of data clusters, while covariance matrices are calculated as an unweighted sum of the covariance matrices of the individual subgroups, minus a factor representing the between-cluster covariance matrix, all assuming a Gaussian distribution. The study demonstrates that the covariance estimates conform to a Stein-type inequality, indicating independence between estimates across different dimensions. Furthermore, it proves that the covariance matrices are a broad family of regularizing functions with a parameter controlled by the number of clusters, effectively generalizing the weighted $\ell_2$-norm. The proposed approach is applied to estimate the regression function and its second derivatives in high-dimensional settings, while also providing a shrinkage estimator for regression coefficients and approximating the posterior variance of a Bayesian linear regression model using empirical data. The method is shown to outperform competitors in estimating the regression function and its derivatives in high-dimensional settings, while providing comparable performance to state-of-the-art shrinkage estimators for regression coefficients.

This research introduces a communication-efficient electric vehicle charging strategy, which prioritizes short-term charging needs and suppresses unnecessary long-term communication. A novel, two-layer architecture was developed, comprising an upper-level scheduler and lower-level controller. The scheduler determines charging sessions, while the controller manages individual sessions, utilizing a deep reinforcement learning approach. The proposed method was evaluated using real-world data and simulated systems, yielding a balance between session numbers and individual session lengths. Results showed this approach outperforms a conventional method under both centralized and distributed communication scenarios, as well as various system sizes.

Accurate predictions of electronic properties are crucial in materials research but are often hindered by the inaccuracies inherent in density functional calculations. To mitigate this issue, researchers employ various density functionals on a daily basis, but the question remains as to which method is the most reliable. This paper presents the DeltaTools suite, a software package that leverages the Delta theory to calculate density functional differences and assesses the reliability of predicted electronic properties. The suite's effectiveness is demonstrated by its application to a range of materials, including metals, semiconductors, and insulators, where it identifies the underlying physical and chemical effects that influence the accuracy of density functional results.

Metagenomic analysis reveals that bacterial communities in diverse ecosystems such as the human gut and oral cavity, exhibit unique compositions characterized by a limited set of dominant species and widespread genetic diversity. To understand this pattern, we developed a model that describes the metabolic niche space occupied by organisms in a multi-dimensional environment. In this space, each habitat or host is represented by a unique set of metabolic characteristics, and each organism by a set of genetic traits, including coding sequences, that define its metabolic behavior. By simulating the evolution of metabolic traits within various habitats, our model shows that the coexistence of dominant species with low genetic diversity and abundant metabolic diversity is possible. Furthermore, our model suggests that the coexistence of competing organisms in multiple habitats can result in the creation of 'host islands' of metabolic potential, where favorable metabolic combinations arise from the interactions between organisms in different habitats.

Building systems can generate an enormous amount of data, significantly higher than what can be effectively analyzed by human experts. This surplus data, however, still holds valuable information that could be leveraged to enhance building management. This research introduces a novel approach, built upon the Symbolic Aggregate Approximation (SAA) technique, to extract meaningful information from data and streamline processing. This technique was applied to building data, such as outdoor weather conditions and HVAC system performance, collected from the University of Nebraska's campus buildings. By using the SAA method, the data was simplified into interpretable forms, such as intervals and piecewise linear functions, which were then analyzed for their practical utility in building monitoring. This simplified data was used to answer common building management queries, including identifying unusual system behavior, analyzing energy consumption, and monitoring indoor air quality. Ultimately, the objective of this research was to demonstrate how simplified models can be used to make more informed decisions when processing and analyzing large-scale building data and its associated data streams.

A hypothesis suggesting that a significant number of hydrogen-poor SLSNe is linked to their binary system origins during a supernova is gaining traction. This theory proposes that mass transfer in these systems may have driven the evolution of SLSNe's progenitor stars towards higher mass loss rates, which in turn could be linked to the explosion mechanisms. To explore this connection, we have developed a binary population synthesis code, which includes a more accurate treatment of mass transfer and the physics of the explosion. Our results show that a significant number of hydrogen-poor SLSNe are indeed produced by binary systems, but with a lower rate of multiple supernovae compared to previous estimates. Furthermore, we have found that a significant number of hydrogen-poor SLSNe are also produced by single stars experiencing an internal core-collapse event. Our study also reveals that a significant number of hydrogen-poor SLSNe are likely to have a single explosion mechanism driving their light curve evolution.

In modern physics, scientific research on magnetic properties in two-dimensional systems is increasingly prevalent. This study focuses on understanding the magnetization dynamics in two-dimensional magnetic systems, specifically investigating the effects of temperature on the dynamic behavior. To this end, the dynamic hysteresis curve and switching time for the Stoner-Wohlfarth model in two-dimensional magnets were examined. The investigation was conducted using a classical Langevin stochastic model and a microscopic spin dynamics simulation method. The results showed that the dynamic hysteresis curve and switching time for two-dimensional magnetic systems are significantly influenced by temperature. Notably, increasing temperature can lead to a decrease in magnetization switching time, but only up to a specific point, beyond which the switching time remains unchanged. This study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of more efficient magnetic data storage devices.

In this research, we explore the development of syntax models that integrate syntax with visual elements. We build upon recent breakthroughs in the syntax of grammar trees, where we combined the best features of two existing models to induce constituency grammar in the context of CLEVR. Our results show that the resulting model excels at explaining visually-related word relationships, surpassing previous studies in syntax, including those that employ graph neural networks and language models. Furthermore, we found that incorporating visual elements enhances the model's performance, particularly when explaining the 'on' relationship.

A common issue in the field of attribution methods is comparing their performance across various datasets, yet despite its importance, there is a significant lack of knowledge in this area. This research investigates the generalization capabilities of six widely used attribution methods when applied to unseen datasets, specifically their tendency to perform well on one dataset but poorly on another. Our analysis involves testing these methods on a new benchmark we have created called \textit{Generalisation on ImageNet}, which consists of a diverse set of 37 classification datasets. Our results show that attribution methods struggle to achieve high correlations with the true labels on test datasets, particularly when compared to training data, with only random selection performing on par with them. Our findings also reveal that certain methods, such as \textit{SHAP} and \textit{LIME}, outperform others, but surprisingly, even the best-performing methods still perform worse than naive random selection on test datasets.

In the context of traversable wormholes in Einstein's gravity, we investigated the formation of double shadows for static, compact, and spherically symmetric objects such as stars and black holes. We found that a wormhole's throat can significantly affect the double shadow's position and shape, particularly by creating additional inner and outer parameters. Utilizing an image analysis algorithm, we studied the double shadow's evolution and its associated physical parameters. We observed that the parameters exhibit distinct variations when objects are positioned at different distances within the wormhole's throat. Notably, the parameters' variations are highly dependent on the wormhole's parameters, including its shape and position. We also found that the physical parameters' trends change depending on the position of celestial objects relative to the wormhole's throat.

We introduce a novel subadditive $\mathrm{Perm}$-estimate for permutations in
finite fields, yielding a significant, three-fold improvement over previously
established estimates in the field by Harper and van Cluneanu. Consequently, this
estimate has the significant implication of providing a linear, deterministic
algorithm for computing the permanent of any non-negative $n\times n$ matrix
with a time complexity of poly($n$). This breakthrough provides a solution to
Krommer's longstanding challenge in linear time complexity, and the issue of
calculating the determinant in linear field size, with the additional benefit of
a linear, deterministic algorithm in this field size. Furthermore, our new
estimate for permutations also enables the solution to multiple combinatorial
problems in linear time complexity.

A family of solvable trimer models on a triangular lattice is presented, and it is demonstrated that they encompass a subset of the Ferrer's general dimer model solutions. By employing a combinatorial approach, we establish the necessary and sufficient condition for these trimer solutions to be admissible. The lattice paths, with certain constraints applied, define these trimer solutions. The study reveals a significant, intricate relationship between the triangular and honeycomb lattices in the context of solvable models. An admissible trimer solution on the triangular lattice can be transformed into a general dimer solution on the Ferrer's diagram. The necessary and sufficient condition for these solutions is also explored through the lattice's triangulation.

This study introduces a model to tackle the target recognition problem in the feature space, where unknown targets are distinguished from known ones based on their proximity to the target boundary. A new distance metric is proposed to achieve this, and the approach is integrated with a generative adversarial network to learn the target boundary in the feature space, ultimately enabling the identification of unknown samples closer to the target boundary. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments in the field of object recognition.

In this research, a novel unsupervised approach is introduced for 3D reconstruction of vehicles from single views. This approach tackles the irregularity issues in existing methods by incorporating a multi-branch CNN that utilizes semantic information to regulate the shape of 3D models. Furthermore, a dynamic alignment module is proposed to enhance the alignment between 2D projections and 3D shapes by minimizing the difference between corresponding features. Additionally, a dynamic consistency module is introduced to ensure that 3D models align with all input images. The effectiveness of the method is evaluated through experiments on real-world benchmarks, resulting in the highest performance to date. The source code of the method will be publicly available.

A key issue in natural language processing is creating query graphs based on a single query and automatically identifying matching entities and attributes in a relational database. Traditional graph-based methods typically rely on handcrafted rules and reorganizing the input, resulting in suboptimal outcomes. To address this problem, a new self-attention-based approach is proposed to automatically construct query graphs and match entities and attributes. By utilizing self-attention to automatically segment both the input sentence and query, this method can identify exact matching entities and attributes in the sentence. Additionally, a self-attention based path model is designed to automatically extract the path structure between a sentence entity and attribute. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate that this method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper outlines a novel approach to developing algebraic models of infinite cryptosystems and their expansions, which can be generalized from existing finite models. An infinite model of the RSA cryptosystem is proposed, and its capacity to transmit information securely over an adversary-controlled channel is examined. An infinite variant of the ElGamal cryptosystem is also explored, along with methods for its constructive generation, from which an infinite model of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol can be derived.

The goal of Named Entity Disambiguation is to accurately identify references in text that correspond to entities in a knowledge graph, ensuring accurate relationships are established. Traditional NED methods can be categorized into two approaches. Firstly, rule-based methods utilize knowledge rules to establish connections between entities and specific relationships based on entity characteristics. Secondly, semantic method relies on calculating similarity scores between entities to determine the correct reference. This study proposes a hybrid approach, combining rule-based and semantic approaches in a single system. The proposed method leverages pre-existing knowledge rules, enabling it to accurately identify potential references, and then applies rule-based and semantic approaches to disambiguate the list. The method's performance is evaluated on the DBpedia-kreuzung dataset, resulting in improved accuracy and a reduction in F1-score errors.

In a non-perturbative approach, we compute the leading quantum corrections to the mass-superficial dimensions of the $S$, $T$, and $U$ in electroweak gauge bosons. These corrections are comparable to the leading quantum corrections to the oblique parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$ derived from the one-loop electroweak radiative corrections. The non-perturbative approach allows for a straightforward derivation of a set of differential equations, enabling the parameter space to be easily explored and analyzed. Furthermore, we identify a specific parameter region characterized by the absence of a mass gap between the Higgs and gauge bosons, resulting in a single mass parameter that governs the parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$. In this region, we find that $S$ and $U$ are directly proportional to the gauge boson anomalous magnetic moment, while $T$ is directly proportional to the difference between the squared Higgs and gauge boson masses. The parameter $T$ is also found to be finite in the degenerate mass limit, unlike its one-loop electroweak radiative corrections counterpart. The non-perturbative approach provides a simplified framework for exploring the parameter space and analyzing the constraints imposed by the parameters $S$, $T$, and $U$.

Dynamic view synthesis from a single video is inherently complex due to the substantial variability in movements, textures, and shapes. The challenge is further compounded by the need to generate new views of non-rigid objects within realistic environments. The key to resolving this issue lies in modeling the intricate interplay between the scene's dynamics and its static components. To this end, we propose a novel approach that leverages the capabilities of implicit representation to learn the underlying scene dynamics and its implicit geometry from a single video input. The approach achieves this by incorporating a prior as a combination of regularization losses that operate directly on the input pixels, thereby allowing the model to learn from high-level features of the input. The model then utilizes a differentiable ray marching module to generate new views of the scene. The results of our evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We establish that the solution Y to the differential equation, whose driving process is the branched rough path G with regularity alpha less than 1/3 plus epsilon, is alpha-homogeneous with respect to G for large G subsequence with regularity alpha plus epsilon. This research builds upon and expands the findings of [Hiu, Kim, Rendel, and Schneider], which proved the same result for the specific case of G with regularity 1/5 plus epsilon.

This research explores the application of a random grain model based on random variables that converge in probability to a normal model, and examines the asymptotic properties of the resulting functions. The study provides closed-form expressions using Charlier polynomials and simpler forms from the Gaussian model, and extends Mehler's formula to this framework. A more general model is also investigated, leading to new asymptotic properties of Gaussian random fields and matrices.

A radio wave reflecting system has garnered significant attention for its potential to revolutionize the implementation of wireless communication systems.  However, the underlying technology still presents several technical hurdles, including the complexity of elements, energy consumption, and data processing latency.  To address these issues, this paper proposes an innovative architecture that integrates radio frequency signal processing at the intelligent reflecting surface (RIS) level.  By employing a reconfigurable filter array, this approach enables the efficient transmission of communication signals and sensing signals on the same frequency band.  To minimize signal processing complexity, this proposal employs a deep neural network to provide meta-data for each RIS element and a neural network-based beamforming scheme for joint communication and sensing.  Simulation results confirm that the proposed RIS architecture outperforms the conventional RIS-based communication system in terms of both communication and sensing capabilities.

We introduce a novel method for coarse-graining a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) using piecewise deterministic processes (PDPs). This method enables us to construct a discrete stochastic process with a tractable transition rate matrix, thereby reducing the computational cost associated with simulating large-scale CTMC models. The method is particularly beneficial as it preserves the simplified dynamics, yielding a model with a limited number of states, lower dimensionality, and reduced memory requirements. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to model continuous-time biological processes, including the regulation of gene expression, protein degradation, and the merging/splitting of vesicles.

Most current studies on low-bit quantization rely on a single phase of training, 
which involves converting a well-trained model from a high-precision version and 
then fine-tuning it for low-bit efficiency. Our research reveals, however, that this 
single phase approach often falls short of expectations. To address this issue, we 
propose an innovative method of cyclic learning that alternates between high- and 
low-bit training to enhance model quantization. Specifically, our method starts with 
high-precision training, followed by a low-bit refinement that corrects errors and 
improves performance. This process is repeated until desired results are achieved. 
Our experiments demonstrate that this cyclic learning approach achieves better 
performance, faster convergence, and more stable training for low-bit quantized 
models. Moreover, we observed that the method can adapt to varying bit widths and 
efficiently find the optimal solution with minimal trial and error.

The double degenerate channel of white dwarf mergers is a possible cause of
certain Type Ia supernovae, with the most current simulations suggesting a
progenitor mass range of 0.8 to 1.2 solar masses. The double degenerate channel
is significantly less restrictive in progenitor mass and mass ratio compared to
the single degenerate channel. Theoretical predictions of the ejected mass from
double degenerate mergers are consistent with those from single degenerate events.
However, the double degenerate channel has the unique ability to produce low
ejected masses. The low ejected mass from the double degenerate channel could be
used to resolve the Lira/Phoenix/3D issues, which involve discrepancies between
the observed and theoretical luminosities of Type Ia supernovae. The ejected mass
from double degenerate mergers can be increased by the explosion, with the
increase potentially exceeding a factor of ten for a certain range of progenitor
masses. The low ejected mass from double degenerate mergers can be used to
explain the faintness of the Lira, Phoenix, and 3D supernovae. The double degenerate
channel of Type Ia supernovae is a promising candidate for explaining the
observed diversity of supernovae luminosity.

In the online learning setting, data arrives in batches, and after seeing each batch, a model is trained before being evaluated. This allows for real-time decision-making based on current knowledge. However, with a limited number of evaluations, the model's performance is often subpar. This research explores how online learning techniques can be optimized with the help of data chunk arrangements. A new strategy, called sequential learning, divides training data into ordered batches that enable more effective online learning methods. A systematic study was conducted to examine how different data distributions affect online learning approaches, especially in the sequential learning framework, using both synthetic and real datasets, and inductive and transductive learning methods. The results show that choosing an online learning method and data distribution are crucial for achieving optimal performance, and that a well-designed data distribution can significantly improve the model's performance.

A novel mobile application, named Green Passport, has been developed to streamline the vaccination process, eliminating the need for individuals to visit a health center to receive their shots. By utilizing near-field communication technology and mobile devices, the application enables secure and efficient storage of vaccination records, thereby facilitating timely administration of shots and allowing users to demonstrate their complete vaccination history and receive a unique digital certificate upon completion of the required shots. This digital certificate can be securely stored in devices such as smart cards and used to demonstrate immunity, serving as a credible alternative to paper-based vaccination certificates and facilitating the monitoring of vaccination progress at the national level. The application's design ensures the highest level of data security, integrity, and confidentiality, as well as facilitating the interoperability between systems, enabling seamless data exchange and exchange between users.

This study examines the relationship between clustering high-dimensional sentence embeddings and categorizing text datasets. Initially, we present a comprehensive review of current techniques that utilize topic-based and language-model-driven clustering methods in the context of sentence embeddings. Furthermore, we provide an empirical analysis combining seven distinct sentence encoders, four different similarity measures, and two clustering algorithms to illustrate the significance of selecting an optimal combination of tools in achieving effective results. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the class topics present within text datasets correspond to distinct clusters formed in the space of sentence embeddings.

We explore the diffusion of a random system consisting of non-interacting particles in a one-dimensional setting, characterized by a time-averaged probability distribution governed by the Sinai model. Focusing on the low-temperature regime where the energy is bounded by a scale Δ, we find that the effective diffusion coefficient Diff scales as Δ^ν with ν = 3/4. This result is achieved by establishing a precise limit on the rate of growth of the effective diffusion coefficient Diff(τ,τ+T) as a function of the time interval [τ, τ + T], where T is a sufficiently long time interval. This generalised limit is also applicable to other algebraic Bernoulli processes.

The spin relaxation of a quantum system, specifically a two-spin-1/2 model, through interaction with its nuclear environment is explored. The system consists of an excited two-spin state and its interactions with nuclear spins and an external environment are modeled. An exact solution to the resulting quantum master equation is found for a specific time interval, allowing for a detailed analysis of the system's spin dynamics. Unlike previously studied cases, this system's relaxation occurs in two distinct phases, with an exponential decay at short times followed by a complex, non-exponential phase at longer times. The behavior of the system's spin dynamics during the initial time period is similar to that of a single spin system, with an Al'tshuler-Aharonov-like phase, but with an added twist due to the interaction with the environment. The system's dynamics are further analyzed through the distribution of the system's spin state, allowing for a detailed understanding of the system's behavior at longer times.

We studied the behavior of a conformal field theory, which is periodically driven and has a non-interacting nature, by employing the replica method and the conformal perturbation approach. Our investigation focused on the return probability, energy density, and specific heat of this system. It was observed that below a certain threshold time, the return probability and energy density display unique characteristics depending on the driving frequency. Conversely, the return probability and energy density above the threshold time exhibit a characteristic pattern of the underdamped mode, while the energy density approaches a temperature-dependent equilibrium value. Moreover, the low-frequency regime is marked by a distinct low-temperature behavior, which is characterized by a power-law decay of the return probability and a linear increase in energy density. Notably, the low-frequency regime is also associated with a non-zero specific heat, which is contrary to the expected behavior in a quantum critical system. Our analysis also revealed that the low-frequency behavior can be accurately described by a classical driven oscillator model.

This letter examines the relationship between compressed sensing and multimodal sensor fusion. We illustrate this connection through a representation learning scenario where a deep neural network is trained on multiple sensor types and we investigate the impact of a single sensor type on existing parameters. Experimental results on the CAR-Net dataset show that neural network parameters acquired during training can be effectively preserved or even improved by adding new sensors, such as radar, and retraining specific parameters. This process enables the fusion of data from the radar and neural network without requiring joint training and optimization.

The Standard Model's $C=\pm P$ violation phase is a fundamental aspect that can be used to search for new physics, with recent advancements in lattice calculations allowing for remarkably precise determinations of $K$-system parameters. A significant step towards this precision is achieved in this study, where we calculate the $K_{\rm L}S$ phase to a high degree of precision, with the results being $\Phi_{\rm KP}^{\rm CP}=(43.5^{+2.0}_{-3.1})^{\circ}$ and $\Phi_{\rm KP}^{\rm CP}=(43.5^{+2.0}_{-3.1})^{\circ}/180^{\circ}$. The results are derived from a large dataset of $N_f=2+1$-quark physics and $N_f=2$-quark effects are incorporated through the use of $O(a)$-improved lattice QCD. The analysis incorporates a comprehensive set of experimental data, with the most significant impact coming from the $K_L\to\pi^+\pi^-$ decay. The results are also compared to those from other lattice calculations.

In a network of interconnected agents, optimal control problems often require analysis under communication constraints. This study proposes a theoretical framework for solving such problems, focusing on a setting with limited, discrete, and bounded communications. It presents two main approaches to minimize the trade-off between communication costs and performance: a planning-based method and a planning-agnostic method. The former method involves creating a complete plan prior to execution, utilizing a path-planning algorithm, and is suitable for applications with low uncertainty and complex tasks. In contrast, the planning-agnostic method uses a reinforcement learning algorithm to adaptively generate control policies in real-time, without prior knowledge of the task. Both methods are evaluated through case studies in multiple robotics scenarios, demonstrating their respective advantages in performance and computational efficiency.

This study focuses on the development of a multi-sensor system that utilizes a Gibbs sampler to model target location probability distributions. The system consists of N sensors with limited communication ranges, each able to detect and locate target objects within their individual areas. By sharing detection data, sensors derive a common probability distribution for target object locations, reducing the uncertainty associated with unknown location values. A probability threshold, denoted as alpha, is applied to generate a labeled multi-Bernoulli birth distribution, which is used in a tracking algorithm to process measurements and minimize the computational burden. A labeled PHD filter is employed to generate target probability distributions, and sensor data is shared to improve detection accuracy. The system's performance is evaluated through simulations, resulting in a 30% reduction in missed detection rates and a 20% decrease in false detections as compared to a standard labeled birth distribution.

The structure of human languages is a complex, interconnected web of characteristics, but current typological knowledge bases tend to focus on individual features in isolation, neglecting their relationships with one another. We propose a novel method for extracting hidden connections between linguistic traits within these databases. By employing a technique called graph autoencoding, which makes use of feature correlations to learn a condensed representation of linguistic characteristics, we successfully apply this approach to the World Atlas of Language Structures dataset. The resulting graph accurately captures the interdependencies between 145 linguistic traits, allowing us to identify previously unknown connections between traits like the presence of cases and the usage of pre-nuclear tonal patterns, and reveal that certain features in WALS tend to appear together, such as zero-case languages and the use of pre-nuclear tonal patterns.

We examine the convergence rates and confidence interval accuracy for two
dominant offline policy evaluation methods: L2R and Target Environments. Our study
compares the statistical properties of these methods using a variety of
simulation-based approaches. Specifically, we investigate how empirical results
match theoretical predictions under different data sizes, reward distributions,
and policy-learning settings, including the scenario of training on one data
set and evaluating on another. Our analysis also yields a straightforward
calculation to determine confidence intervals for policy evaluation.

The conventional method of calculating fermentation output in bioengineering is based on partial differential equations that take into account a pulse input and solve a well-established initial value problem. However, these models fail to account for the inherent variability in biological systems, leading to significant errors in predictions. To address this limitation, we propose a Bayesian approach that incorporates prior knowledge from experimental data to reduce model uncertainty and estimate a comprehensive parameter range. Our method involves solving the partial differential equation with uncertain initial conditions and provides a comprehensive solution rather than just an instantaneous one, and the results are demonstrated through multiple case studies that showcase the effectiveness of this approach in managing fermentation output variability.

In the polaron theory, the effective mass that influences the energy of a polaron and the quadratic momentum term can be related to each other. Research suggests that these two parameters are not entirely independent and that they are connected through the relationship between the electron's interaction with the phonon system and the acoustic properties of the material. Studies have shown that for materials with positive elastic constants, the effective mass that influences the polaron energy increases when the phonon interaction strength grows, whereas in negative elastic constant materials, the reverse is true.

The electric flux through a closed surface is time-dependent and influenced by magnetic fields.  The magnetic field strength in a force-free electrodynamics environment determines the duration of the electric flux.  We establish a connection between the electric flux and the expansion of a star's magnetic field.  We investigate the relationship between the electric flux and the expansion of a star's magnetic field through a closed surface.  We derive a formula that relates the magnetic field strength, expansion rate, and duration of the electric flux through the closed surface.  We apply our formula to the Sun's magnetic field, using its mean radial expansion rate, and find that the electric flux from the Sun is approximately 10^9 times shorter than its surface flux.  We conclude that the electric flux from the Sun is short-lived, and its electric field is very strong.  We calculate the electric field at the Sun's surface, finding that it is approximately 10^8 times stronger than the surface electric field.  We establish a connection between the electric flux and the expansion of a star's magnetic field, and find that the electric flux from the star is long-lived, and its electric field is very weak.  We calculate the electric field at the star's surface, finding that it is approximately 10 times weaker than the star's surface electric field.  We find that the electric flux through a closed surface is determined by the surface electric field.  We establish a connection between the electric flux and the expansion of a star

Schr\"odinger's cat is in a superposition, where it's both alive and dead at the same time. This paradoxical concept is a result of a quantum object interacting with another object placed outside the Schr\"odinger framework. A different approach to understanding quantum interactions involves the concept of resource theory, which views a quantum system as a valuable resource. In this context, Schr\"odinger's cat is a vast quantum resource. Using the principles of resource theory, we can apply the concept of "free" quantum systems that interact with Schr\"odinger's cat. This leads to the development of a time-invariant Schr\"odinger cat representation, which can be experimentally verified through the use of entangled atoms in different energy states.

We investigate the intricacy of the patterns formed by dividing a periodic function f into m periodic components using the formula $f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m f_j(x)$, specifically focusing on minimal unique parts. Building on Szabados's conjecture, we examine how the divisors relate to the components of the function. The results indicate that an upper limit on the total components of the function is proportional to the total number of divisors when the function is divided into components of order one, but this limit no longer applies in cases of higher-order components. To further analyze the relationship between the function's components and divisors, we introduce a new measure of the function's intricacy and explore its behavior in various scenarios.

The Gromov-Hausdorff distance serves as a continuous measure of the dissimilarity among the characteristics of bounded metric spaces. In this study, we establish that the distance between two bounded metric spaces, as determined by Gromov-Hausdorff, is equivalent to the distance as defined by the cut distance in the contexts of spaces with a finite number of points and those with product structures. Our findings are grounded in the connection between the Gromov-Hausdorff distance and the Kantorovich distance, a relationship that enables the exchange of information between these two metrics.

We examine the resolvent of the $m$-divergence form elliptic operator in a two-dimensional domain with a smooth boundary. Given a small parameter $\varepsilon$, and assuming certain conditions on the coefficients, we derive an asymptotic expansion for the resolvent in the case where the spectral parameter lies within a specific strip in the complex plane, ending in a remainder term with an order of $\varepsilon^{2\tau}$ for any positive value greater than one. This result enables the construction of an exponential resolvent approximation up to a remainder term with an order of $\varepsilon^{2(\tau-1)+1}$.

Recent studies have shown that using explicit dialogue states improves performance in task-oriented dialogue by providing a public benchmark dataset and demonstrating better results with joint optimization and explicit training data and states. However, we argue that training with formalized states is more effective in achieving higher performance, as it offers a more detailed and structured annotation scheme compared to the loose and unstructured turn information. To address this, we introduce a new training method that leverages formalized dialogue states and demonstrate its effectiveness by achieving higher performance on the standard benchmark dataset. Specifically, we achieve an average optimal dialogue score of 2.67, a 3.7% increase over the current state-of-the-art model's score.

Software developers utilize Software Model Checkers (Smt-Switches) to implement conditional execution paths in their code, essentially creating an executable version of the code with the conditions relaxed. However, this approach has a significant drawback as it increases code size, leading to substantial overhead during execution. To address this issue, we introduce Smt-Switch, an optimized compiler that leverages hardware multithreading to condense the code, by only executing the code that corresponds to the conditions that can be executed in parallel. By doing so, Smt-Switch enhances performance and the overall speed of applications that rely heavily on Smt solving, resulting in a significant average speedup of 2.6 times.

We have developed a new, efficient way to find the eigenstates of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian, which is crucial in various systems. Our approach, based on projecting the potential onto the orthogonal set of polynomials, has been tested in the context of Bessel potential. Notably, this method exhibits superior stability and faster convergence for states that don't follow the quasi-exactly solvable pattern, whereas its performance for quasi-exactly solvable states is comparable to other established methods. Our proposal holds the most promise for applications in the regime where quasi-exactly solvable states blend with continuum spectra.

Deep neural networks are often designed to process input data at a fixed resolution, but this approach can be overly rigid and not reflect the natural process of image formation. A more flexible approach is to allow these networks to adapt to varying input sizes, but this can be problematic if the network's behavior changes excessively with different inputs. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach by temporarily expanding the network's input resolution, and then downsampling it to its original size. This can be viewed as a form of image filtering, which can be achieved by convolving the input with a kernel of higher resolution before downsampling. To make this process more efficient, we use a technique called the running average of pixel expectations (RAPE), which enables the use of a smaller kernel and lower computational costs. Additionally, we show that RAPE can be viewed as a form of regularization that reduces the number of parameters required by the network. To make this process more efficient, we use a technique called the running average of pixel expectations (RAPE), which enables the use of a smaller kernel and lower computational costs. RAPE can also be combined with other techniques, such as pixel hopping, to further improve its performance. In our experiments, we find that RAPE outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches in various tasks, including image classification, segmentation, and object detection, and is particularly effective in reducing the number of parameters required by the network.

The presence of p-mode oscillations in a binary star's secondary component significantly affects the dynamics of convective cells on its surface, particularly when the binary's orbital frequency matches the cell's rotation period. Observations of such secondary effects can provide insight into the secondary's dynamical state. This study examines how p-mode oscillations influence the dynamics of convective cells on a rotating star and evaluates the relevance of observed $pF\ell$ oscillations to theories of convective cell rotation. We find that a secondary component with a dynamical state similar to that of HD 199478 B, such as a main sequence star or a white dwarf, will exhibit convective cell rotation periods of $1-2$ hours, regardless of its mass. In contrast, a star with a dynamical state similar to that of a subgiant or main sequence star with a convective core will have higher convective cell rotation periods, often exceeding the binary's orbital period.

We have established that scalar-electromagnetic clouds, which are charged scalar field configurations that surround black holes, can exist in spacetime, regardless of the black hole's mass or background environment. Our research focuses on "self-interiating" scalar field clouds that emerge from a specific type of potential, and we have found that they can form around black holes of any size, whether massive black holes or those resulting from the merger of black holes and/or compact objects. This finding is particularly significant, as it challenges a common assumption in physics that these types of black holes should be stable, free from gravitational waves, and governed by a simple set of physical laws.

We investigate how the CP-violating phases of active neutrino-sterile neutrino mixing might be constrained or determined, focusing on a scenario with three active neutrinos and one sterile neutrino. We consider a specific model where the sterile neutrino couples with $Z'$, which is generated by $SU(2)_L$ singlet Higgs fields. The analysis involves the contributions of neutrino-sterile oscillations and $Z'$-mediated neutrino decays to the constraints on these CP phases. Furthermore, we explore how the sterile neutrino's Yukawa coupling and $Z'$ mass can be constrained by the same constraints.

We introduce a new generative adversarial network, denoised with a specially designed, deep convolutional neural network, capable of handling various types of noisy input data. This approach, built upon the concept of contrastive learning, aims to extract noise patterns and remove them from the input data. A key component of our method is the CVF module, which enables the network to identify clean images within its training data and separate them from the noisy input. This is achieved through a unique loss function that incorporates a contrastive loss, which facilitates the identification of noise and the subsequent removal of this noise from the input data. Our experimental results, which involve the use of deep convolutional neural networks, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in handling both Gaussian and impulse noises. Furthermore, we showcase the robustness of our method by applying it to images featuring both types of noise in conjunction.

We address the challenge of determining the number of rows A required for successful 1-norm sparse recovery from a given matrix A, known as the information-computing complexity, by establishing a tighter bound for its k-sparse variant. This bound, dependent on the smallest singular value of A, exhibits tighter performance, specifically a logarithmic factor improvement compared to previous methods. Additionally, we provide an explicit, constructive solution for the optimal matrix A that achieves the tightest known bound, demonstrating the importance of the smallest singular value of A in resolving the complex optimization problem involved.

In recent years, the use of contracts in functional programming has gained momentum. Building on ideas from research in linear logic and dependent types, contracts allow a more precise modeling of a program's expected behavior. However, the complexity of certain operations like union and intersection is increased by considering contracts at a higher level. This paper explores a potential solution to this issue by introducing a simpler concept of higher-order contracts, allowing for a more streamlined model. Furthermore, this paper provides a precise description of the semantic properties of higher-order contracts, derived from the behavior type type, and demonstrates the main results within Intensional Linear Logic.

We've developed a reinforcement learning model that leverages insights from
psychological studies involving human motivation. By incorporating a dual
approach to motivation - both internal and external factors - our model shows
enhanced performance in training. By utilizing policy gradient methods, we've found
a notable improvement in policy performance through the integration of these
motivational components. Furthermore, our model's modular design enables the
separation of training processes, thereby allowing for increased flexibility and
control over the training procedure.

We investigate the convergence of series solutions to time-independent Schrödinger equations with an anharmonic potential, using the ground state of the Schrödinger equation as a reference and expanding around a correct perturbative point. The correct expansion parameters are determined by matching the zeroth approximation to the exact solution. The correct expansion parameters depend on the frequency of an oscillating force that is periodically varied in time. We derive the correct expansion parameters by solving the stationary Schrödinger equation, using the oscillating ground state as a reference. We then derive the correct perturbative series by expanding around the correct parameters, ensuring that the zeroth approximation has the correct energy and satisfies the correct zeroth approximation to the stationary Schrödinger equation.

Our research focuses on the computational methods for determining the contributions of specific topological structures in quantum gravity using the BV formalism. In contrast to previous studies, we find that the contributions from various topological structures are not additive. When evaluating two-point functions, we observe that the primary structure's contribution is significantly enhanced, while the effects of other structures are significantly reduced. As a result, the two-point function's behavior is primarily influenced by a single structure, with the effects of others becoming negligible. Conversely, for the tetrahedron partition function, the contributions from multiple topologies are substantial, and their intricate interplay is crucial for understanding the result. Notably, the result cannot be explained by the individual contributions of these topologies, suggesting that the complex relationships between them are vital for understanding the result.

To assess whether Twitter's suspension policy effectively reduces rule breaches, we analyzed the patterns of suspended users before and after the action was taken, comparing them with a group of non-suspended users who maintained an active account. Our findings showed a noticeable decrease in rule-breaking instances among suspended users; however, the rate of rule-breaking among the suspended users remained higher than that of the active user group. We also discovered that the majority of rule rule-breaking occurred by the suspended users and not by the active users in a shorter timeframe of 1 day after the action was taken, indicating a significant impact on reducing rule-breaking among suspended users within a short period. Conversely, the effect was less pronounced in larger timeframes of 1 to 7 days.

The rapid advancements being driven by LHC research are also expected to influence the development of LHC instruments and those at its own energy level. This contribution will present some ideas on how the next generation of accelerators might contribute to both e$^-$-hadron and hadron-hadron physics experiments, possibly leading to the establishment of facilities by the mid-2020s.

This research introduces an innovative approach to neural networks that can effectively learn from data with uncertain labels by utilizing ensembles of mini-networks. Our approach enables the network to accurately identify uncertain labels by leveraging the collective output of its ensemble units. Composed of units with smaller network dimensions, the ensemble can process input data in parallel, producing a probability distribution over the possible labeling space. By aggregating the probability distributions from each unit, the network achieves a robust classification outcome, even in cases with incorrect or incomplete labeling. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in a variety of challenging data sets, such as medical diagnosis and gene expression, by delivering consistent predictions and conformal inference in response to data perturbations.

This study examines the prioritization of resources in V2X communications for safety-critical vehicles under limited infrastructure support. A scenario is considered where a high-risk vehicle is approaching a collision-prone area, for instance, a pedestrian crossing an intersection. A proposed resource allocation method selects the most critical events from various vehicles and the pedestrian based on priority, choosing the highest-priority event when resources are available. Prioritization is achieved by assigning higher values to more critical events, such as vehicle-pedestrian collisions over vehicle-vehicle collisions, by giving vehicles a higher value than non-vehicles. A proposed resource allocation metric is then used to select the most critical events from vehicles and pedestrians. Simulation results show the proposed resource allocation method has a lower delay compared to existing methods, like vehicle-to-vehicle priority, while still providing lower reliability for non-critical events.

The rapid advancement in AI has sparked concerns over its ethical implications, with particular worries centered around algorithms designed to interpret and predict human thoughts and emotions. Advances in off-the-shelf emotion recognition tools, despite their convenience, must be scrutinized in light of their potential for both societal good and harm. We aimed to assess the existing tools for their ability to demonstrate bias, with a focus on the impact of cultural differences. A large, culturally-diverse dataset was created with two distinct annotation approaches, which we then used to compare emotion recognition software in a controlled setting. The findings revealed notable disparities in accuracy rates and a strong potential for algorithms to be influenced by the annotator's perspective, highlighting the need for ongoing evaluation of AI systems.

This research examines the relationship between feature toggles and the management of feature branches. Our hypothesis is that the use of feature toggles can influence the efficiency of resolving merge conflicts among branches, the number of branches that need to be merged, and the effort required to merge branches. To investigate this, we analyzed data from 12 projects in the Z3 repository, comparing changesets that involved feature branches with those that did not. Our findings indicate that using feature toggles has no significant impact on the efficiency of resolving merge conflicts or the effort required to merge branches. However, we found that the adoption of feature toggles was associated with a decrease in the frequency of branch merges, leading to a larger number of changesets being maintained by each branch.

Our investigation into the relationship between symmetry and conservation reveals
that accidental symmetry, as seen in Hamiltonian systems, provides insight into the
conservation of enstrophy in the Navier-Stokes equation. By examining the dynamics
of enstrophy, we understand that conservation is broken by boundary effects and
vortex line breakage, ultimately leading to its dissipation. Notably, these events are
highly unlikely and therefore described as "accidental." Furthermore, the emergence
of accidental symmetry, as influenced by boundary effects, helps explain the
transition from three-dimensional to two-dimensional behavior in turbulent flow near
a wall.

Most people assume feature maps alone aren't enough to grasp how a deep network extracts and combines features, but we show that the Maximum Attention visualization, derived from attention maps, offers valuable insights into the forecourt's focal points. By leveraging the gradients of a target output, the Maximum Attension approach enables network exploration without requiring activation functions or input data. It can be applied retroactively to pre-trained networks, allowing users to investigate how a specific object might be processed, independent of input data or network configuration. We applied the Maximum Attension approach to an Image Classification network and an Object Detection network, demonstrating its potential for understanding how these networks process the scene. Our findings indicate that the Maximum Attension approach is more effective than other existing methods in understanding Feature Extraction, as it is independent of network architecture and activation functions, and doesn't rely on input data.

Recent discoveries in particle physics and cosmology have underscored the necessity of incorporating novel phenomena at low energy scales. This involves considering the production of massive particles with spin-2 characteristics and their subsequent impact on the behavior of the Higgs boson. Theoretical frameworks predicting the presence of such particles necessitate the inclusion of their characteristic loop effects in calculations. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive calculation of the loop effects stemming from massive spin-2 fields in the process of the Higgs self-energy, utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence. The calculated effects are presented in both momentum space and momentum representation, with a focus on the potential for these fields to be detected at the LHC.

The decision of whether to engage in a war or negotiate for peace is influenced by various factors, such as the state's military strength and political position. Although the impact of political bias has been acknowledged, its effect on the outcome of negotiations and wars has not been thoroughly examined. This study investigates how political bias influences the CIGAR model's predictions of war and peace negotiations. The analysis indicates that political bias distorts the state's perceived strength and the number of states involved in a negotiation, leading to increased expectations of a successful peace agreement and decreased expectations of a successful military campaign.

A fundamental aspect of language comprehension is assigning meaning-based associations
between words, such as those indicating the relationship of actors to objects, in
sentences. Researchers have employed various methods, including functional magnetic resonance imaging, to
study how the brain assigns these connections. In contrast, a new approach involves
analyzing how different types of brain activity overlap when processing these
connections. Using electroencephalography, researchers examined how subjects
understood sentences with two different word orders, such as "The man hits the woman" and
"The woman hits the man", by looking at brain activity in three distinct time frames:
early processing, when subjects were making predictions, and when they actually saw the
words. Results showed overlapping brain activity in two distinct areas of the brain,
which are involved in making predictions and actually processing language, which
suggests that these areas are working together to comprehend the meaning-based
connections. This overlap was observed in regions of the brain that are typically
involved in making predictions, such as the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in
processing language. This overlap was particularly evident when subjects were
examining sentences with two different word orders, which is consistent with the
idea that these areas are working together to comprehend the meaning-based
connections.

The detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and Virgo has opened a new field of multi-messenger astronomy. This research aims to improve the accuracy of the source localization for gravitational wave neutrino candidates. The current AIC-based method for source localization is used to generate initial trigger maps from the Gravitational Wave Open Data and is then compared to the performance of the Bayesian Source Localization method on these events. The results show significant improvements in both the speed and accuracy of source localisation when using the GSL method for specific neutrino candidates.

The spatial Point Spread Function (PSF) distortions known as mirror seeing, caused by an aspheric primary mirror's aberration, can be mathematically modeled and linked to the spatial PSD amplitude. This model is founded on a linear relationship between the spatial PSD amplitude and the primary mirror's asphericity error, as seen in the Von Karman spherical aberration (VKS) mode. By applying this relationship, we can determine the seeing from the PSD, and conversely, derive the PSD from the seeing and the mirror's asphericity error characteizer, then simulate the seeing PSD using a fast Fourier transform. This method was successfully applied to the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope's PSD data from 2019-2020.

The accuracy of phonon dispersion is crucial for understanding material stability and physical properties. This study investigates the applicability of the r2SCAN density functional in predicting phonon dispersion, focusing on the relationship between this functional and the random phase approximation. By comparing the r2SCAN results to those obtained from the random phase approximation and experiment, this work evaluates the functional's performance across a range of materials, including insulators, semiconductors, and metals, using a variety of methods.

This paper presents a novel method to calculate coverability sets for very-WSTS (well-quasi-structured transition systems) by developing an algorithm that reduces the problem to reachability in finite systems. The approach is demonstrated through the computation of coverability sets in monadic unification problems, yielding a new algorithm for solving this problem. The developed method also enables the construction of coverability graph encodes, a coverability test for very-WSTS that is compatible with a broader class of Petri nets.

The primary objective of the AGES project is to investigate the fluctuations in the characteristics of active galactic nuclei (AGN) over extended periods. To accomplish this, the project utilizes a 1.84 m dome-enclosed telescope at the Lijiang Observatory, a 250-meter dome-obsatory in Yunnan, a location known for its exceptional, clear skies. The variable nature of AGN makes studying these objects challenging over an extended period. To mitigate this challenge, the project incorporates cutting-edge technology, including a custom-built, 1.84-meter telescope with a 1.3 m focal length, designed to facilitate high-resolution spectroscopy and high-speed, follow-up photometry. The project also employs a UV-Vis telescope with a 1.3 m focal length, paired with an 8000s-1s (1s:16ms) readout system, capable of capturing high-cadence spectra. The data collected by AGES is thoroughly analyzed, utilizing a comprehensive data analysis pipeline, consisting of a sophisticated system for evaluating, processing, and characterizing AGN spectra. The project's primary objectives are to investigate the inherent variability of AGN over extended periods, identify rare and unusual phenomena, and provide essential data to constrain theoretical models.

The process by which quantum systems give rise to objective, classical realities is a fundamental question in the transition from quantum to classical. Quantum Darwinism, a novel theory proposed by Zurek, offers new insights into this complex issue. This book provides an in-depth examination of Quantum Darwinism, including how it distributes information, how the environment influences this distribution, and how it ultimately leads to the formation of objective realities. The text also delves into the broader implications of this theory and its connections to other areas of physics, including information transfer and quantum coherence.

This paper develops a method to calculate tight bounds of the reachable set for discrete-time dynamical systems affected by random disturbances. A novel approach is presented by representing the reachable set as a sequence of convex bodies, enabling the derivation of its Hausdorff and convex hull measurements. Building upon this method, an ellipsoidal bound can be obtained through iterative application in scenarios where the convex hull measurement remains consistent. A key benefit of this method lies in its ability to compute tight bounds without prior knowledge of the system's parameters, applicable to scenarios including discrete-time linear systems with zero-mean Gaussian disturbances.

The SAINT model, a cutting-edge pre-training technique for tabular data, has garnered significant attention. Yet, its performance in certain tabular data tasks remains inferior to traditional machine learning methods. We propose a novel approach, SAINT-G, a generalized SAINT model, capable of enhancing tabular classification and regression performance across various tasks, particularly when traditional machine learning methods excel. By incorporating a novel pre-training objective, SAINT-G leverages the power of tabular data row similarities, resulting in improved representation learning.
