Our proposed OPSED method achieves a balance between model accuracy and communication efficiency by incorporating an exponential downweighting mechanism that reduces the influence of outdated model updates. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates the efficacy of OPSED, which outperforms conventional federated learning methods, particularly in scenarios with high device turnover rates.

Predicting dialog acts on current utterances is a fundamental component of understanding
user intentions. Most current models rely solely on the preceding statement,
overlooking the preceding short discussions. We propose a straightforward yet
effective approach to incorporate the preceding short talks into our
dialog act prediction model. Specifically, we suggest a multi-layered
graph-based architecture, where each short talk is represented as a separate node,
and the current statement is connected to these short talks. We demonstrate the
model's performance on the Multi-English Short Discussion Dialog Act dataset,
showing its superiority over single-turn based models and previous graph-based
models.

We have developed a comprehensive model for a telecentric etalon-based spectrograph to investigate its capabilities and performance. This model allows us to explore various design trade-offs and enables straightforward optimization and optimization modifications during the design process. We have created multiple scenarios to explore different aspects of the spectrograph's design. A custom instrument was designed with a 4-inch aperture and a focal ratio of 5.3, and its performance was compared to a standard collimated spectrograph design. Furthermore, the model was used to assess the sensitivity of the instrument to manufacturing inaccuracies and variations in its components' optical properties.

In the first main finding, we investigate labeling all the points within an n-set with p-colored unit disks within an n by p grid with the minimum number of disks requiring at least p minus one new disks. This is done by showing that for any n points, a compatible labeling with only one edge necessitates at least p plus five new colored disks. In the second main outcome, we explore labeling all the points within an n-set with p-colored unit disks and p colored line segments to achieve a labeling with at most six colored disks. This is accomplished by constructing a specific labeling with three point labels and six line labels on an n-set with three colored disks and three colored line segments.

In this paper, we introduce Codelet, a novel program execution model for chiplet architectures, and Codelet-7, a prototype chiplet leveraging the Codelet model. Codelet represents a program as a collection of Codelets, which are groups of computational tasks that can be executed on different chiplet components. Codelet connects these tasks with inter-device communications and data transfers. Codelet-7 implements Codelets as hardware accelerators and introduces a streaming interface that enables efficient data transfers and communications between devices. By reorganizing the execution flow of popular workloads, such as ML, video processing, and virtual reality applications, into Codelets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Codelet-7 in improving system performance.

A popular technique for improving prediction accuracy through presmoothing is widely applied in classification and regression, but its relevance to survival analysis remains poorly understood. This study investigates the benefits of presmoothing in survival analysis, utilizing real-world and simulated data to compare its effectiveness with maximum likelihood estimation. Our findings demonstrate that presmoothing can significantly enhance prediction accuracy by as much as several percent. A key factor in this improvement is the reduction of the maximum likelihood estimator's bias, allowing for more precise and efficient predictions. Building on this discovery, we present a robust, data-driven approach for selecting the optimal presmoothing parameter.

A metric nonlocal transitivity matrix is used for defining the nonlocal metric nonleaves and nonlocal hyperbolicity index of graphs. The nonlocal metric nonleaves are defined as having a metric nonlocal transitivity matrix with a zero row or column, while graphs with a nonlocal metric nonleaves or a metric index equal to 1 or n(G) - 2 are considered nonlocal hyperbolic. Additionally, graphs with a metric index equal to 1 or n(G) - 1 are considered nonlocal hyperbolic. Notably, trees fall under both categories. More specifically, complete bipartite graphs have a metric index equal to 1, complete graphs have a metric index equal to n(G) - 2, and graphs containing a vertex of degree n - 2 have a metric index equal to n(G) - 1. The study further explores the relationship between the nonlocal hyperbolic index and the diameter of graphs, with an emphasis on identifying the complete bipartite graphs and cycles achieving the highest nonlocal hyperbolic index on a diameter of 2.

This study delves into side-channel attacks on MNIST-based neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, specifically examining how power trace measurements of the Adam optimizer reveal sensitive information about both the data and the model through their correlation. By developing an attack involving a differential power analysis, we successfully retrieve the initial values of the first and second momentum memory elements and the weights for a majority of the data classes. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique to recover the training data labels from the input data alone, utilizing either the entire power trace or a single power trace measurement, and achieve an 80% accuracy rate in doing so.

To achieve a reduction in polarization's impact on signal quality, we have developed a method that systematically assesses how far a given polarization profile can be shortened without significant loss of information. By establishing lower and upper limits on the partial distances within a set of nested polarizations, we can determine the optimal number of iterations for the shortening process. The resulting method not only guarantees that shortening is possible without significant loss of information but also provides a strategy to achieve an accurate lower bound. The strategy involves constructing a specific polarization profile using the polarization profile in question. The resulting method is versatile and can be applied to various scenarios, including the estimation of any function, the regression of a vector-valued function, and the classification of a vector-valued random variable. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we have provided a simple example that demonstrates its practical applicability.

We have developed a straightforward, component-wise denoising method rooted in autoencoding principles. To enhance the effectiveness of this self-supervised denoising process, a synthetic dataset is employed for an initial stage of supervised training. Subsequently, the pre-trained model is refined using unsupervised techniques on actual data. This approach yields a straightforward, versatile model capable of processing data at high resolution. Due to its component-wise structure, the method is well-suited for processing data in various formats, such as 2D sections, 3D volumes and other forms of time-series data. We have successfully tested this approach on a diverse dataset including seismic data from different time periods, such as 2D seismic reflection data and 3D OBC seismic reflection data.

In this study, the effect of real photon emission in lepton-proton scattering processes is investigated in the context of charge asymmetry within the one-photon approximation. The analysis considers both positive and negative virtual photons and their impact on the scattering of a muon off a proton. The findings indicate that the contribution of real photons to the charge asymmetry is directly proportional to the squared muon beam polarisation, thus highlighting the significance of muon polarisation for real photon emission. The results also show that the real photon emission enhances the magnitude of the asymmetry up to 2.5% and the asymmetry measurement could be a viable method to investigate the parton's hard-gluon matrix element.

A three-dimensional Mott insulator, characterized by a large gap in its electronic spectrum and exhibiting a unique spin-polaronic ladder structure, has been synthesized with a cobalt-based compound, showing a substantial impact on the material's electronic and magnetic properties. Furthermore, this ladder spectrum is highly responsive to both an applied magnetic field and external pressure, which can lead to the observation of reentrant behavior in the material's magnetization. A theoretical model has been developed to account for the experimentally detected phenomena, with results indicating that the material's reentrant magnetization can be attributed to the competition between spin and charge interactions.

We address the challenge of estimating treatment effects in situations where the treatment is not restricted to a discrete set of values. To accomplish this, we develop two novel estimators that utilize the inverse probability of coping test results. These estimators are grounded in local parametric modeling and maintain key robustness properties. Notably, one estimator is resistant to misspecification, while the other is also resilient to the misspecification of the treatment function. Furthermore, we provide conditions under which asymptotic normality and a central limit theorem apply. A simulation study demonstrates the effectiveness of our estimators in a real-world setting.

Recent research on starshades has gained significant momentum, prompting a cross-disciplinary workshop to explore the potential of recent breakthroughs and drive future discoveries in this area. This report provides an overview of the Starshades Workshop, which took place in person and virtually from November 9-12, 2020. The report includes a summary of the scientific motivation, workshop objectives, and key outcomes.

Previous suicidal text datasets were often limited by their biased sampling methods, which only included texts with confirmed suicidal outcomes, thereby failing to capture the complex dynamics of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Our Robin dataset, on the other hand, utilizes an unsupervised approach to collect suicidal-related text from social media platforms. By crawling online resources and using search terms related to suicidal behavior, we developed a dataset that not only contains confirmed suicidal texts but also texts indicating suicidal ideation, stress, anxiety, depression, or other related topics. Our dataset, consisting of over 170,000 tweets with more than 460,000 associated words, provides a comprehensive understanding of suicidal-related language and offers a valuable resource for researchers. Our analysis of the dataset highlights the effectiveness of the Robin dataset in capturing diverse suicidal-related words and demonstrates its utility in identifying suicidal texts through sentiment analysis.

A supersymmetric version of the Schwarzian action has been developed through two distinct methods. Firstly, the action was derived by extending a solution to a matrix model within the boundary theory of three-dimensional chiral supergravity. Secondly, it emerged as a general solution for a class of integrable super-Schwarzian functions, subject to constraints related to space-time supersymmetry. In both cases, the resulting action is identical and demonstrates that the constraints on the super-S Schwarzian function are inherent. This action was then used to analyze the holographic principle in supergravity, yielding a precise model of the AdS2 with a specific isospin Lie algebra.

Researchers in mathematics, mathematics education, and computer science are interested in rational dynamical systems and linear difference equations.  We've developed a novel tool that utilizes rational algebraic properties to identify the orbits of these systems.  This method has practical applications in solving linear and quadratic equations, as well as determining the orbits of rational dynamical systems.  It's noteworthy that the same approach works for orbits of specific systems involving second- and third-nearest neighbor shifts, which connects linear dynamics to areas such as the theory of subshifts and the statistical properties of low-complexity strings.  We've also established a link between the period lengths of linear dynamical systems and the growth of the solutions to linear difference equations.  We've further expanded upon these findings by generalizing their applicability to the orbits of general rational dynamical systems.  We've also demonstrated that the orbits of these systems coincide with the solutions of specific linear difference equations.  We've also established a connection between the period lengths of these systems and the growth rates of their solutions.  We've also developed a method to determine the orbits of these systems using their characteristic polynomials.  We've also applied this approach to the study of the 3-neighbor shift, which is a specific type of subshift that has been extensively studied.  We've also made a connection between the orbits of these systems and the growth of the solutions to linear difference equations.  We've also established a link between the period lengths of these

This paper examines the phase behavior of a Reissner-Nordström Anti-de Sitter black hole, which is coupled to logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics and axion dynamics, and explores its phase transition diagram in the canonical ensemble. By analyzing the critical behavior, we demonstrate that the logarithmic nonlinearity and axion dynamics have a significant influence on the electrodynamics theory and the black hole's thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the logarithmic nonlinearity and the Born-Infeld nonlinearity, which is a well-known nonperturbative theory, and discuss the canonical ensemble phase transition diagrams for both theories.

We consider a linear form $f(x)$ with integer coefficients $a_1, a_2,...,a_k$ and an infinite Sidon set $S$. We show that for almost all sets of sequences $1\leq |S_N| < cN^{\delta}$ of positive integers, where $\delta > \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2k}$, there exists a subset $S_N$ such that the number of solutions to $f(x) \in S_N$ is asymptotically equal to $\frac{|S_N|}{N}$ for a constant $c > 0$. This generalizes previous results of van der Corput, Bourgain, and a 2012 finding of the first author, which both addressed the case of $|S_N|$ close to $cN$.

A theoretical investigation into geometric quantum phase transitions in spin systems is conducted, focusing on the Ising model in a two-dimensional lattice. By employing the transfer-matrix method and analyzing the partition function, the ground-state energy and magnetic properties are derived as functions of temperature and external magnetic field. A novel susceptibility measure is introduced to detect first- and second-order quantum phase transitions. A relationship between magnetic susceptibility and geometric phase is established, indicating that the latter serves as an effective indicator of quantum phase transitions. By examining the effects of lattice size and boundary conditions on susceptibility, a geometric parameter is proposed that characterizes the lattice's shape and influences susceptibility.

A theoretical model analyzing the behavior of ferromagnetic systems as they cool from high temperatures has been developed. This model takes into account the critical fluctuations common in systems undergoing phase transitions and is based on the master equation approach. By deriving mean characteristics from the theoretical model, such as correlations and critical exponents, and comparing them to the standard mean-field model, it becomes clear that critical fluctuations significantly impact the systems' critical behavior. Furthermore, the model reveals a new critical behavior in systems affected by critical fluctuations, which is distinct from the usual mean-field critical behavior and is supported by numerical simulations of a one-dimensional Ising model.

Recent research has shown that quasicrystals can exhibit unique properties due to their structure, such as the 10-fold symmetry in 2D or 12-fold symmetry in 3D, resulting from the Bragg scattering of electrons off the lattice. However, when electrons interact with each other, their behavior changes significantly. A study on a model system of interacting electrons bound to lattice sites in a quasicyral structure found that localization occurs when single particle states are localized. However, this effect is significantly altered when electron-electron interactions are considered, leading to the breakdown of lattice symmetry and the transition from quasiperiodic to localized eigenstates. Our research shows that the critical interaction strength for this transition is influenced by the lattice structure and the lattice filling. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the presence of electron-electron interactions can suppress or even induce localization in single particle states, providing new insights into the behavior of electronic systems in quasicrystals.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages are typically trained using human-annotated data. However, this process is time-consuming and costly, and recent neural models require vast amounts of high-quality data to be effective. To address these challenges, a novel method is proposed that utilizes a large-scale, machine-automated data generation process. This involves translating existing mono-language datasets and combining them into a multilingual dataset. A pioneering generation system is also introduced that utilizes a large-scale, mono-language dataset to produce semi-structured task-oriented dialogues in multiple languages. The proposed system is compared to traditional multilingual dialogue systems trained on human-annotated data and a zero-shot baseline. The results show that the proposed system achieves comparable performance to the best existing models, and significantly outperforms the zero-shot baseline.

RNA-seq time series analysis can uncover complex biological mechanisms such as gene regulation through differential splicing and expression. A new R package, rnaseqTSS, is designed to analyze RNA-seq time series data, offering a range of statistical and graphical tools. These include the ability to estimate gene abundance, determine differential expression and expression change, and identify significant splicing events. This package also allows for the visualization of gene or transcript abundance profiles and provides a graphical interface for comparing gene expression levels across multiple samples. Additionally, rnaseqTSS facilitates the comparison of gene sequences across different time points and provides a cluster analysis to group genes based on their similarity.

Technical measures implemented to protect data privacy often rely on complex legal frameworks, making it essential for legal experts and engineers to collaborate closely. Yet, their interactions frequently become convoluted due to the distinct nature of their disciplines, leading to costly errors and decreased trust. Through a qualitative study involving 31 interviews with professionals from legal and engineering fields, we discovered that their varying backgrounds and approaches to work impede effective communication. By understanding these differences, we can develop more effective solutions to optimize the interaction between legal and engineering experts who design data protection measures.

We've investigated the azimuthal correlations of two and four particles in a heavy ion collision context, utilizing the Color Glass Condensate formalism to derive our findings. Our research built upon the work of tributes to a deceased individual, by introducing specific correlations within a globally color-symmetric state in both two- and four-particle scenarios. Furthermore, we established connections between these findings, degree of freedom counting, and previously proposed correlations in a $2\to 2$ kinetic theory framework.

The initial production of light composite particles such as deuterons, helions, and tritons is analyzed for Au + Au and Pb + Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV using the AMPT model. This model shows that coalescence is a major factor influencing the production of these particles, particularly at high rapidity and transverse momentum. Deuterons and helions' transverse momentum spectra are found to be more sensitive to the initial Au + Au collision geometry than their production yields. Furthermore, the transverse momentum spectra of these particles are more accurately described when accounting for the effects of event-by-event fluctuations in the initial Au + Au collision geometry. In contrast, the production of tritons is less affected by these fluctuations.

The presence of multiple rocky exoplanets within a system raises intriguing possibilities for their atmospheric compositions, particularly given their shared formation and environmental conditions. Investigating the atmospheric characteristics of these exoplanets will be crucial in determining the habitability potential of each world. Our research focuses on the atmospheric implications of the TRAPPIST-1 system, where we analyze the effects of atmospheric loss and the accumulation of volatiles on nearby planets. Our findings indicate that the expected atmospheric diversity among the TRAPPIST-1 system will be relatively low, with diverse compositions primarily resulting from variations in the atmospheric escape rates of the exoplanets rather than differences in their formation environments.

The study of Boolean functions, particularly those expressed by monomials, has been a significant focus in various fields. Researchers have extensively analyzed the characteristics of Boolean functions, their degree of dispersability, and circuit size of depth two, in the context of the complete hypergraph. In contrast, there has been relatively less attention paid to the same properties within the framework of hypergraph structures.

In this paper, we investigate the properties of Boolean functions, within the specific framework of the $d$-dimensional hypercube, in the context of $d$-partite hypergraphs. We introduce a new measure of dispersability for Boolean functions, in the context of $d$-partite hypergraphs, and demonstrate its connection to the same measure in the context of complete hypergraphs. We analyze the properties of the measure within the context of $d$-partite hypergraphs and demonstrate that, for a particular class of hypergraphs, namely, those derived from circulant graphs with jump lengths not exceeding 3, the properties of the measure are identical to the properties of the same measure in the context of complete hypergraphs. We leverage this connection to derive the exact circuit size of depth two for a particular class of Boolean functions, in the context of the 3-dimensional hypercube, and further establish a relationship between the measure and size of circuits in the context of $d$-partite hypergraphs.

To address the non-convex regularized sparse recovery problem, an alternative to the nested svr algorithm is presented using a new approach called nested neumann, based on the neumann series. It's shown that this new algorithm achieves a convergence rate of O(1/(r^k) + O(1/r^k)) where r represents the depth of the inception complexity for the objective function's gradient. Furthermore, a new proof for the nested svr algorithm's convergence rate is given, as it also relies on the depth of inception complexity for the objective function's gradient.

This study examines the impact of cosmic friction term on the boost phenomenon in single-field inflationary models, particularly the effects of the coupling between the inflaton and the metric. The research initially outlines the basic principles of boost, then explores its behavior in the presence of cosmic friction term. The analysis reveals that the presence of cosmic friction term can significantly reduce the boost, which is primarily attributed to the interaction between the inflaton and metric. Notably, the reduction in boost caused by the inflaton-scalar field interaction is due to the cosmic friction term's ability to increase the rate of curvature perturbation growth. The research also investigates the boost mechanism in the presence of cosmic friction term for two specific inflationary models, namely the Higgs-like and quadratic inflation models, and concludes that the boost effect is highly sensitive to the cosmic friction term's presence.

Airline revenue management is focused on selling flights at the highest prices, which can be influenced by offering previously unavailable fare options. Traditionally, to ensure fairness, airlines only sell fares that have already been booked. However, there is a possibility to offer a previously rejected fare to the current highest bidder without compromising fairness. Research suggests that by doing so, airlines can increase demand and earn more revenue, but at a cost. The potential economic benefit of this approach is what motivates the sale of tickets. We develop a model to determine the price of selling a ticket, which takes into account the airline's potential revenue from selling another ticket to the same passenger at a higher price. We find that offering a rejected fare increases the sale price of the original ticket. We also analyze how this approach affects passengers, identifying those who benefit from it and those who do not. We model the airline's decision-making process using a two-stage model, which captures the passenger's decision to buy a ticket in the first stage and the airline's decision to sell it in the second stage. We find that the airline should only sell a previously rejected fare to passengers who would have bought the original ticket at a higher price. We develop a method to determine the price of selling a previously rejected fare, which takes into account the passenger's utility. We find that this price is higher than the passenger's willingness to pay, reflecting both the airline's revenue and the passenger's utility. We also find that offering a previously rejected fare to

The casebase package streamlines the analysis of survival data by incorporating a new estimation approach, which considers time-dependent factors. This approach yields more accurate results by utilizing random sampling from pre-existing casebase datasets, thereby eliminating the need for time-dependent covariates to be fully observed. Additionally, the package facilitates the estimation of parameters under both uniform and log-linear probability conditions, allowing for the calculation of variance-based estimates and confidence intervals. Casebase's functionality is demonstrated using real-world and hypothetical datasets, showcasing its ability to handle weighted casebase samples and incorporate covariate selection through regularization techniques. Furthermore, the package's compatibility with existing estimation methods is highlighted, particularly in conjunction with the popular Cox-Proportional Hazards model.

A novel semi-numerical method for solving the Schrodinger equation has been developed. This method incorporates an analytical solution to a perturbation expansion and a numerical approach to a modified Hamiltonian. By combining these methods, the semi-numerical approach enables efficient solution of complex problems with minimal computational cost. The method has been applied to the Hulthen potential to find numerical solutions, and the findings were verified through comparison with other existing results. Furthermore, the semi-numerical approach has been extended to multi-dimensional systems, and the results for a three-dimensional Hulthen potential with spin-orbit coupling were found to be accurate and reliable, outperforming other available semi-classical and numerical techniques.

In recent years, object storage with its flat, flat hierarchical model has become increasingly popular for big data applications, despite the traditional use of POSIX file systems. However, the scalability issues inherent in traditional POSIX systems make them unsuitable for modern big data demands. To address this, the NBBFS system was developed - an object storage-native file system that leverages standard POSIX interfaces. By employing an efficient metadata management system and taking advantage of object storage features, such as data replication, NBBFS is able to achieve high-performance scalable file systems. The results of extensive testing on large clusters demonstrate NBBFS's ability to handle high workloads and scale effectively.

In urban areas where electric vehicle (EV) adoption is on the rise, there's often an insufficient supply of charging points. This study explores how auction-based pricing mechanisms can be used to allocate limited charging resources in multi-service parking facilities for electric vehicles. We analyze the effectiveness of different pricing methods in minimizing the number of drivers forced to leave their vehicles without a charge after parking. We examine two types of scenarios: one where parking and charging costs are separate, and the other where they're bundled. We compare the performance of online pricing mechanisms, including the uniform pricing, second-price auction, and uniform pricing with priority, methods using a simplified model of parking and charging demand. The results show that these pricing mechanisms can efficiently manage a limited supply of charging resources to minimize the number of drivers left stranded after parking.

Our research yields two original methods for creating new Hermitian Low-Density Parity check (LCD) codes from existing ones, including code expansion and code fusion. The initial technique generates a code expansion by producing a longer code with a maximum distance of at least five, from a Hermitian LCD code of length n, resulting in a code of length 2n+1. The resulting codes have optimal LCD parameters and exhibit strong group-cyclic properties. The first method to generate these codes is a generalized version of the expansion method, applicable to any LCD code. The second technique, code fusion, generates new Hermitian LCD codes of length 2n+2 by merging the dual codes of two length n codes. These codes have optimal LCD parameters and exhibit strong group-cyclic properties. Additionally, we have generalized the fusion method to create new codes of length 2n+2 from any LCD code of length n.

Calculating the black-hole scattering amplitude for Einstein gravity paired with a scalar field at the fourth order requires the computation of corresponding effective worldline actions. Our study extends this process by determining the complete set of analytically computable integrals up to the sixth order. At the sixth order, an analytically computable integral that depends solely on black-hole solutions is identified, along with a non-integrable inadmissible integral that emerges at this order and cannot be eliminated through integration. The presence of this integral of distributional nature prompts a revision of the initial assumption that all required integrals can be eliminated.

The rapid growth of solar and wind power in the US has led to increased land use risks for these energy sources, making it difficult to meet clean energy goals. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been proposed, but their effectiveness remains unclear. Our study combines a linear programming model of the US electricity market with a stochastic site selection model to assess the impact of land use risks on achieving a 60% and 100% renewable energy portfolio. Our findings indicate that these risks result in significantly higher costs to achieve these targets, with a 60% renewable energy goal in 2050 costing $221 billion, compared to $173 billion without land use risks. Our analysis also reveals that limiting site selection to specific states can further exacerbate these costs. Our results provide valuable insights for policymakers seeking to balance the benefits of renewable energy with the associated land use costs.

Cluster-randomized trials frequently employ the outcome approach to measure treatment effects in clusters, rather than for individual subjects. In these trials, treatment-induced outcomes in each cluster are compared to a shared control group. We examine how to estimate the direct impact of a vaccine from the outcome approach, revealing that this estimation is unfeasible. We subsequently develop a resampling-based method for determining a confidence interval that closely approximatesively estimates the specific direct effect of the vaccine. This approach is validated through a Monte Carlo simulation and an analysis of an HIV vaccine trial.

This study proposes a comprehensive framework for calculating the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index and other topological indices of networks based on their structural properties. The degree-Kirchhoff index is a specific type of topological index that can be expressed as the product of various graph indices, including the degree sequence and the Kirchhoff index. Since the graph indices are inherently linked to the structure, it is possible to develop an end-to-end mapping scheme to compute the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index and other topological indices of networks. The proposed mapping scheme is applied to various well-known topological indices of networks, and the results are validated through case studies of several real-world complex networks.

We investigate contextual linear bandits where both agents and learners are equipped with knowledge of the context distribution. In this setting, we analyze how learners' knowledge of the context distribution affects communication requirements between agents and learners. We find that with perfect knowledge, contextual communication complexity is directly proportional to the context distribution's effective dimension, allowing learners to make more accurate predictions. However, when learners must estimate the context distribution, their uncertainty leads to increased communication requirements, with dimension dependence being secondary to that of estimation. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel online contextual least squares algorithm, OCL, which leverages knowledge of the context distribution to achieve improved regret and communication requirements. We demonstrate that OCL achieves a sub-linear regret and communication rate, with the latter being minimally influenced by context distribution parameters.

The widespread occurrence of class imbalance in real-world predictive modeling tasks has driven research into addressing this issue. Current methods to balance class distributions aim to correct the imbalance, but this approach can be problematic as it does not consider the unique probability distribution of data observed during testing. In response, we propose a novel strategy for reclassification that, when combined with oversampling techniques, can effectively counteract the effects of class imbalance. Our approach involves adjusting the predicted labels during training by utilizing the imbalanced data's label distribution, which ultimately aims to minimize the discrepancy between the training and testing data's label distributions. Through extensive evaluations in various settings, we show that this method can be used to reverse the impact of class imbalance and improve model performance.

The Standard Model's accuracy can be tested through precise measurements of particle decays at the LHCb experiment, providing valuable information for a variety of research areas. This includes refining the angle gamma in the Standard Model, detailed insights into charm mixing, and potential discoveries in charm CP violation or the observation of rare top decays. This presentation will focus on the potential for vector-tensor decays in beauty and charmed baryons and beauty mesons, offering valuable information for independent verification of particle decays within the Standard Model framework.

A significant number of research fields utilize statistical methods to analyze data and make predictions. However, these studies often rely on assumptions that may not always be valid. To address this problem, researchers have developed new methods for identifying and quantifying potential biases in their studies. In particular, a technique called quantile coefficient of variation has been shown to be effective in measuring uncertainty in various data distributions. To further develop this method, a new algorithm has been designed to provide more precise and accurate results, especially in situations with diverse data sets. The proposed algorithm has been tested on various scientific datasets and has been found to be effective in detecting biases and making accurate predictions. The proposed algorithm has been found to be effective in situations with diverse data sets and has been found to be effective in detecting biases and making accurate predictions. The proposed algorithm has been found to be effective in situations with diverse data sets.

A versatile technique for controlling high-power, nanosecond X-ray beams is introduced. This innovation, known as 'flying focus X,' enables a precise scanning and focusing capability by harnessing X-rays emitted from a nanostructured X-ray tube (XANDE) traveling at high speed. Focusing the X-ray beam allows for enhanced resolution of various laser-based applications, including high-resolution X-ray microscopy for complex materials and biological samples. Our method offers flexibility in optimizing X-ray focusing based on the desired resolution and sample size. This technique's potential also extends to high-throughput imaging and analysis of large-scale biological samples.

The FIRA HuroCup league, consisting of humanoid robots, has been conducting annual competitions since the 2000s without ever having a standard, universally accepted virtual or artificial intelligence opponent. To address this gap, a new virtual opponent called HuroBot has been created to participate in the tournament. The proposed HuroBot system is designed to provide a realistic simulation of a humanoid robot for the official tournament. In order to effectively utilize the new virtual opponent, the decision-making strategy was optimized through the implementation of a Q-learning algorithm. The research also explores the impact of different reward systems on the performance of the HuroBot. The findings reveal that the traditional non-linear reward system significantly enhances the virtual robot's performance and achieves a high success rate of over 80% in the 2021 tournament's scenarios.

The cross-domain recommendation (CDR) issue is being tackled by an increasing number of researchers, however most existing studies have been centered around the assumption that the two domains share the same data distribution. This paper proposes a new CDR framework called CAIR that integrates both conditional adversarial learning and metric learning to enhance its ability to capture the underlying data distribution. By combining these two techniques, CAIR first generates a shared representation that aligns the data from both domains while also leveraging the benefits of metric learning to preserve their inherent similarity distance. This allows CAIR to model the data distribution more effectively, and as a result, deliver superior cross-domain recommendation performance. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate CAIR's superiority over existing state-of-the-art techniques, showcasing its ability to generalize across different domains.

In the classical model of finite-state machines, the method of communication, or how information is exchanged, has a significant impact on a machine's capabilities. As a result, different machine types are capable of recognizing different languages.

The primary goal of this research is to develop a new finite-state automaton model that maintains a significant degree of flexibility in its capabilities, yet effectively reduces the method of communication to a single, standardized method. To achieve this, we introduce a novel automaton model that combines state and external communication as integral components, effectively merging two previously distinct approaches into a single, comprehensive framework. This new model, referred to as the state-communication automaton, enables the development of a universal state-communication net, or SCN, that can simulate any state machine or communication automaton with equivalent expressiveness.

A novel method for heat transfer analysis in two-dimensional complex plasma layers is introduced. The model incorporates the effects of a confining two-dimensional potential and takes into account the vibrations and rotations of particles. An equation describing the probability density function of their positions and velocities is formulated. The model also examines the impact of a steady-state, non-uniform heat source and a linearized collision operator on the probability density function. The scenario of a confined plasma layer exposed to an infrared laser was studied in more detail.

This paper introduces a method to assess the expressive capabilities of certain machine-based systems, specifically counter machines with unlimited storage, by translating them into equivalent Petri net-based systems. The paper then utilizes this translation to compare the capabilities of these machine-based systems, with one system found to encompass the other. The paper concludes by establishing the equivalence between these two systems.

To improve image quality and reduce processing costs for coronary angiography videos, a new low-dose super-resolution deep learning model is presented. This model, called the Low-dose Super-resolution Network for HFRCA (LSRnHFR), is designed to create high-quality, 60 fps videos from low-dose, 30 fps X-ray angiography sequences. Two types of data were used to train the model: a simulated dataset and real-world coronary angiography data. The model achieved high-quality video results with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 40.95 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.96, outperforming a previous method by 7.1 dB and 0.13, respectively. Real-world experiments confirmed that the model effectively restored both the spatial and temporal details of coronary angiography videos.

The precise measurement of rare heavy-flavoured particle decays is a key aspect of the FCC-ee project. The experiment takes place in an exceptionally controlled background environment, minimizing interference from cosmic rays and internal radioactivity. The minimal background noise allows for the precise detection of particles at very low frequencies, making rare events more detectable. Furthermore, a specialized containment system, combined with efficient electromagnetic shielding, significantly reduces background counts, paving the way for a new generation of rare decay experiments at the FCC-ee project.

Neutrinos, as particles interacting through the weak force, can provide valuable insights into new physics beyond the Standard Model, complementing dark matter searches. Neutrinos can be detected by measuring the interactions between nuclear recoils, but the challenge lies in distinguishing them from the background caused by the interaction of dark matter particles. The recent discovery of a significant enhancement in neutrino-nucleus scattering by the PERC project offers new possibilities for dark matter research, particularly in direct detection experiments. We demonstrate that this enhancement can potentially lower the detection threshold of dark matter and improve sensitivity to its mass, allowing for the exploration of the WIMP parameter space. Furthermore, the enhancement may also contribute to the resolution of the 'nuanced mass split' problem in supersymmetric models, making it easier to identify WIMPs with masses around 10 TeV.

The gravitational influence of an intermediate-mass companion on a star orbiting a supermassive black hole causes the star's orbit to change in a specific way. We have identified a connection between this change and a particular type of stellar phenomenon called a pulsar magnetosphere, where the star's rotation induces a distinct build-up of energetic particles near its surface. Our research suggests that the star's orbit will cross the region where this phenomenon occurs, resulting in a sudden disappearance of its radiation observed from Earth, which could last around 10 to 20 years. The rare and unusual nature of this event could help explain the recent observations made by the CHIME/FRM2 telescope of a fast rotation observed in PSR J0030+0451, which could last up to 20 years and start again in the future.

This study investigates solutions to SDEs that are perturbed by fractional Brownian motion, with a focus on the impact of the Hurst parameter. We aim to demonstrate the existence of a transition semigroup, establish a strong mixing property, and estimate the total variation distance of the solution. Our results show that the characteristics of the solution are heavily dependent on the Hurst parameter $H$ and the starting point $x$. Specifically, when $H$ is less than or equal to $1/4$, the solution exhibits pathwise uniqueness and strong Feller properties similar to Brownian motion. In contrast, when $H$ exceeds $1/4$, the solution has a more complex behavior, including a significant decrease in the total variation distance of the solution as $H$ approaches $1/2$, even when the starting points are distant.

We demonstrate that a nonstationary ideal over ω1 can be represented by a Σ1 formula parameterized by a set if, and only if, it is countably complete and has a countable ideal of countable cofinality ω1. This result provides an answer to a question asked by Hrusak, Iovino, and Lasko, additionally showing that the truth of the conjecture's negation results in the existence of a stable ultrafilter that can be defined by a Σ1 formula parameterized by a set, a fact proven by Kanovei and Lavezzari.

Multitask training is known to significantly improve task performance, but the optimal way to conduct this training varies greatly depending on the specific tasks. This disparity makes it difficult to establish guidelines for multitask training. Our research suggests that a crucial factor contributing to its effectiveness is the ability to cross-analyze task behavior at different levels. To investigate this idea, we introduce the Multitask Behavior Tree, a tool that utilizes various levels of detail to track the progress of multitask training. Our analysis demonstrates that utilizing this tree can lead to the creation of adaptable strategies for multitask training, resulting in improved performance on multiple tasks. Furthermore, we examine the possibility of automating the creation of these strategies using meta-learning techniques.

The development of large-scale traffic sign datasets has been instrumental in refining object detection algorithms, particularly through the use of transfer learning. A robust dataset enables researchers to effectively leverage domain-specific knowledge and optimize algorithm performance. In this study, we present Traffic-SigV2, a comprehensive dataset that surpasses its predecessor in terms of scale and diversity. As one of the largest traffic sign datasets available, it has been designed to support deep learning-based solutions with extensive training data. It includes over 180,000 images containing more than 450 categories of traffic signs, collected from 24 countries around the world. Our research outlines the collection process, provides an in-depth analysis of the dataset, and showcases its potential for enhancing traffic sign detection and classification models through transfer learning.

Conventional supervised methods for top-k recommendation require substantial labeled data, which is often time-consuming and expensive to obtain. This paper introduces SelfCF, an innovative framework that enables top-k recommendation without any explicit supervision. SelfCF leverages self-supervised learning to significantly reduce training time while delivering comparable recommendation accuracy in comparison to traditional methods. This is achieved through self-retrieval and temporal sequence modeling, which allows for the creation of task-specific data augmentations and capturing of sequential patterns within implicit feedback. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on multiple benchmark datasets have shown that SelfCF yields superior recommendation performance in a remarkably shorter training time – just 15 minutes with 10 million data samples, in contrast to 3 hours with 10 million data samples.

The objective of this study is to create a more comprehensive approach to counting covers of a curve, which involves considering the effects of specific ramification conditions beyond ordinary ramification. We achieve this by leveraging a previously established framework, namely ramification PETs, to incorporate these conditions and derive a unified formula for the total sum of all ramified covers. This unified approach enables the separation of non-ramification conditions into distinct categories, leading to a deeper understanding of the underlying combinatorial principles.

We have investigated the electronic structure of a gapped Dirac semimetal, specifically the gapped gDGM, by employing a four-band tight-binding model. The results show that the density of states and optical conductivity exhibit a peak at high energies due to momentum conservation, resulting in a band crossing. The application of an external electric field induces interband transitions, which can be described by the polarization-dependent absorption spectrum. Notably, the gDGM's anisotropic optical conductivity is highly dependent on the polarization direction. Additionally, the absorption spectrum is sensitive to the mass value of the fermions, with a notable shift towards lower energies.

We analyze a specific mathematical equation describing how population dynamics change over time, with varying and periodic coefficients that affect the behavior of solutions. The equation is based on previous work which showed that these dynamics could either stabilize or grow indefinitely, depending on how fast they change. We're interested in how these dynamics are affected by an additional factor that slows down the behavior of the solutions. As this slowing factor increases, certain characteristics of the behavior of solutions are observed, including how solutions might converge towards a stable state, and how solutions near a stable state behave in terms of their size and frequency.

We have developed a new method to calculate the coefficients of the polynomial expansions of the tidal deformability in a post-Newtonian effective one-body model. This method was used to obtain the polynomial expansions for black hole binaries of non-spinning or spinning black holes. Our results show that for a binary black hole to produce both the (3,3) and (4,4) modes, it must have a total dimensionless spin of at least 0.55 for third-generation gravitational wave detectors. Additionally, our findings indicate that the (3,3) mode is more sensitive to spins than the (4,4) mode for low-mass binaries. We also found that including spins in a binary black hole's tidal deformability leads to a more complex distribution of the (3,3) mode. Lastly, our study reveals that the (4,4) mode is more significant for detecting binary black hole merges with high spins.

A new method for detecting and characterizing astrometric binaries is proposed, focusing on the initial angle at which the companion star is visible. The initial angle is directly related to the companion star's orbital period, the star's distance, and the observing location. Our approach was tested using data from the Hipparcos mission and applied to a specific type of binary known as type-III, characterized by a long orbital period exceeding 1,000 years. The results revealed 14 new type-III binaries and 13 potential candidates, and we found that the initial angle can be used to identify systems containing a black hole companion, with 4 systems matching this condition. The discovery of these systems supports the existence of low-mass black holes and provides new insights into the formation of binaries with very long orbital periods.

To effectively apply evolutionary algorithms, one must carefully consider the key parameters including population size, the range of mutation values, and the parameters of the crossover operator. In this study, we explore the effectiveness of different crossover and selection methods within a population, focusing on the performance of these algorithms in solving the well-known 0/1 knapsack problem. The results of our experiments indicate that utilizing uniform crossover alongside a binary tournament selection method enables our algorithm to achieve the fastest convergence rate. Additionally, our findings highlight the importance of adjusting the mutation probability in accordance with the population size in order to optimize performance.

This research examines the $L^2$ quantization of two-dimensional oscillatory integrals with or without polynomial components in the Fourier analysis context. It demonstrates the existence of an upper limit on the $L^2$ magnitude for oscillatory integrals with smooth phases and derives a specific estimate when phases involve polynomials of a specific degree. Notably, the derived bounds outperform those found in previous studies on the $L^2$ quantization of classical oscillatory integrals with polynomial phases.

The benchmark for automatic detection of hate speech across Arabic languages established a standard evaluation protocol, with a shared task at the ARHES workshop, building on the existing ARHSE shared task from 2018. In this research, we present our team's contribution to the shared task, focusing on the classification of hate speech in social media posts, specifically in the Arabic norm form. Our approach combined the predictive power of two leading models, DistilBERT and Longformer, with the RoBERTa language model, achieving high accuracy in three subtasks. Our team secured first place in classification and binary detection with optimal results of 0.872 and 0.799 maco F1 respectively, while second place was achieved in named entity recognition with 0.744 maco F1. Our findings indicate that Longformer outperformed DistilBERT and RoBERTa in classification and binary detection, but the RoBERTa model excelled in NER, highlighting the diverse performance of these models on different subtasks.

The recent development of Quantum Monte Carlo on the Continuous-Time Random-Phase Approximation exchange-correlation kernel has led to significant advancements in the field. Building upon this work, we have now extended the approach to calculate not only energies but also forces for molecules. Our findings indicate that the computational cost of these calculations increases with the effective pseudopotential charge of the valence electrons, which we found to scale quadratically with the number of electrons. This is in line with our findings for energy calculations. Our new method has been successfully applied to various molecules, including those containing transition metals, which we found to yield results in good agreement with traditional first-principles calculations.

The dissemination of false information via social media, particularly Twitter during the 2020 US election, posed significant concerns about its impact on voter trust and national stability. Twitter initially blocked several prominent Twitter accounts, including that of President Trump, in an effort to combat the spread of misinformation about voter fraud. However, existing methods for detecting such false claims relied on rule-based rules that were often incomplete or required manual enforcement. In response, we developed a new, more accurate and efficient approach to detecting false information, leveraging a combination of machine learning, graph analysis, and natural language processing. By integrating these techniques, we created a system that effectively identifies and flags accounts that engage in voter fraud misinformation, and which we used to study the spread of such false information among Twitter users, revealing a complex pattern of dissemination.

We have demonstrated in a recent paper that for a specific class of probability measures $\mu$, associated with a one-dimensional expanding map $T$, points of high emergence according to the measure $\mu$ possess a Hausdorff dimension that does not exceed $\dim_H T^{-1}1 + \mu_Y$ and this conclusion holds under the assumption that $\mu$ has a SRB property.

Deep Bayesian neural networks are typically resource-intensive, hindering their application in large, complex domains. To mitigate this issue, we've developed an approach that leverages variational autoencoders to create efficient, reduced-dimensional representations of high-dimensional data. By incorporating these autoencoders into the Bayesian neural network, we enhance its scalability without compromising performance. Additionally, we've devised a new local ensemble regression technique that significantly accelerates posterior inference. Experimental results reveal that our method yields results comparable to the original high-performance network while achieving a substantial 10-100 times speedup.

The theory of instantons provides a strong theoretical framework for understanding the mechanisms of reactions involving many-body tunneling processes in both chemical and biological systems. However, the application of instantons is often hindered by the complexity of the reaction environment, making it necessary to simplify the system to incorporate quantum effects back into the theory. We propose a novel approach to incorporating instantons in such complex systems, using a quantum environment that is coupled to its degrees of freedom. This approach is illustrated through its application to the electron transfer reaction in the charge qubit, where the instanton formalism is used to calculate the reaction rate.

This research introduces a straightforward, model-free strategy to enhance the control signals generated by predictive controllers for robots. Based on predictive control theory, the strategy aims to eliminate the discrepancy between predictive models and reality, minimize overshoot, and accelerate convergence to setpoints. By incorporating precomputed offset terms into the control system, the method can be easily integrated into existing feedback control loops. This solution is adaptable to various robots and control systems. Furthermore, the method can be effectively combined with machine learning-based controllers, such as those utilizing neural networks, to improve its performance. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through both simulation and real-world testing, specifically for a 6-degree-of-freedom industrial robot arm.

We have investigated the thermoelectric coefficients of a tungsten-based $\kappa$-(ET)2Cu$_{2}$O$_{2}$ alloy doped with 2.5% W, utilizing the tight-binding model in conjunction with the Boltzmann transport theory. The incorporation of W introduces a low-energy band within the gap, which significantly affects the material's electrical and thermal properties. As a result, the alloy exhibits a notable enhancement in the thermal conductivity due to the introduction of a low-energy conductivity band, while its Seebeck coefficient is diminished. Furthermore, the introduction of the W-based conductivity band amplifies the thermoelectric figure of merit.

The perfect sum problem, a classic example of computational challenges, involves finding two numbers within a specified range that add up to a given target within a specified time limit, often demonstrating the limitations of algorithmic efficiency. However, by applying probabilistic principles, it has been demonstrated that in the perfect sum problem, the optimal solution to the problem of finding two numbers closest to a given sum within a specified set can be achieved more efficiently than previously thought, contradicting the assumption that any further speed-up in computation was not possible.

Let $a$ be an element from the multiplicative group of a finite field $F_m$ and $k$ be a positive integer less than or equal to $m-1$. We utilize elements formed by dividing $x^m-a$ by its irreducible polynomials of degree $k+1$, to construct new finite fields $F_m[a]$ extending $F_m$. We then find the optimal value of $k$ that yields the extension $F_m[a] = F_m(\gamma)$ with $\gamma$ being a root of $x^m-a$. Furthermore, we find that $F_m(\gamma,\zeta)$, with $\zeta$ being a primitive $3$-rd root of unity in $F_3$, has a maximal order of $m3$ if $m$ is not divisible by $3$, and a maximal order of $m$ if $m$ is divisible by $3$.

This research introduces an innovative method for creating strategies to optimize the efficient utilization of software resources. The approach is founded upon the application of modern model checking techniques and a novel, graph-based model of sequential programs that effectively captures the essential behavior of loops and parallel execution. The new synthesis method has been successfully demonstrated through the development of strategies for intricate models derived from real-world parallel programs, including a Java program like the Easymind example, and those with high levels of parallel execution, such as a program with 64 parallel threads.

In this study, we have developed an advanced metasurface imaging system that can capture fine details in noisy conditions. Two key aspects of this system are its ability to increase resolution in inverse problems and improve the efficiency of sampling in imaging inverse source distributions. We have demonstrated this concept with a simulation where a 2D inverse source was imaged using a 16-element metasurface. By adjusting the input wavefront, we were able to capture both spatial and temporal properties of the source, resulting in high-fidelity inverse solutions. Furthermore, we have shown that this system can operate with only 7/16 of the input wavefront samples, even in noisy environments. To achieve this, we have integrated a deep neural network with a physical model to optimize sampling schemes for metasurface imaging systems.

The population of hydrogen's Rydberg states can be controlled by specific laser fields, as shown by varying the population in a hydrogen atom exposed to different combinations of laser pulses. The varying strengths of these pulses affect the population at different Rydberg states. To control the population, we investigate the effects of two pulses with different durations, frequencies and polarizations. The first pulse excites a specific transition, while the second pulse modulates its intensity to control the population transfer to other Rydberg states. By adjusting this second pulse's duration, frequency and phase relative to the first, we can control the population at various Rydberg states. This approach is useful for directing excited states in a 3D atomic gas, such as guiding them to detectors or trapping them in optical lattices.

To enhance semi-supervised learning in image segmentation, our proposed method creates customized training datasets by modifying specific areas within unique image datasets. This generates a diverse set of mixed samples with distinct characteristics, including texture, color, and shape. By using an algorithm to generate these mixed samples, the algorithm can be trained on a mixed dataset and then applied to individual datasets with varying levels of labeled information. This approach allows for the combination of data from different sources, increasing the amount of available training data and improving performance. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in comparison to existing techniques, including prototypical networks and pseudo-labeling.

This study introduces mathematical models based on the chemical master equation for simulating the dynamics of gene expression in prokaryotes and prokaryotes with CRISPR-Cas9 systems. By utilizing these models, optimal experimental designs can be determined to maximize gene expression variability. Furthermore, the impact of various parameters on the performance of experiments is examined. In addition, the study provides a data analysis method for evaluating the success of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, using the $\Delta$-operator to identify and quantify system parameters. This approach is applied to experimental data from the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing of human T cells.

In many machine learning applications, graph-based learning methods are employed, and the structure of these graphs often plays a crucial role in their performance. While learning node hyperparameters can improve the performance of learning algorithms, the learning process itself becomes computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we propose a new learning approach that allows for the learning of graph structures within the training process. We develop a method to optimize graph learning based on the structural similarity between two graphs and introduce a training algorithm that incorporates graph learning as an additional objective. Additionally, we introduce a new structural similarity measure that can be efficiently computed and integrated into the learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed algorithm through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world data sets.

In the field of quantum computing, the hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), has gained significant attention for its potential in solving complex optimization problems. Researchers have conducted an in-depth study on how QAOA, trained using stochastic gradient descent, is impacted by errors commonly found on near-term quantum devices, including relaxation and imperfect measurements. We investigated the effects of another type of error, coherent dephasing, on QAOA, using both numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. We found that, unlike other types of errors, the presence of coherent dephasing errors significantly affects the training process of QAOA, including its ability to reach the optimal solution and the relationship between the training speed and step size. Furthermore, our results indicate that, in the presence of coherent dephasing errors, the optimal depth of QAOA changes depending on the step size used for training, providing valuable insights for the practical implementation of QAOA on near-term quantum devices.

The field of Person Re-Identification has gained substantial interest due to its vast potential for use in various surveillance systems. However, its practical application is hindered by the lack of large-scale datasets collected in real-world scenarios. This study introduces a novel dataset, called UniVision, consisting of 10,378 images from 51 individuals captured in real-time university settings. To enhance the accuracy of the Re-ID task, our proposed approach integrates a Siamese-CNN based extractor with a RBF-Kernel-SVM based re-identifier, and employs clustering techniques to reduce the massive feature space. Additionally, our study utilizes the UniVision dataset to evaluate the performance of the Re-ID extractor and extractor, and to compare the efficacy of the extractor and re-identifier. The results show that UniVision outperforms other large-scale datasets in terms of Re-ID accuracy.

The increasing use of machine learning and data-driven methods in power systems planning and operations has created a need for high-quality data sets to effectively evaluate these techniques. However, generating large data sets in power systems is often a labor-intensive process due to the intricacies of real-world systems. To address this challenge, we introduce a data generation framework that enables the creation of complex power system time series data with customizable attributes. By leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks, our approach can effectively replicate the temporal patterns observed in real-time power system time series data. Additionally, our framework includes a set of tools that facilitate the analysis and visualization of the generated data, allowing for the explicit identification of system stress and fluctuations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by successfully producing and analyzing a synthetic data set for the Western Interconnected system.

This study explores novel iterative methods for resolving variational inequality issues, with given data assumed to be well-defined. Novel iterative methods derived from the proximal Lagrangian and Tykhonov regularizations are presented, along with a comparison of their theoretical properties. Key convergence results are obtained, indicating that the general iterative sequences converge to the set of optimal solutions when the regularization parameter approaches zero. Additionally, it is shown that the general iterative process from proximal forces and Tykhonov forces converges to a unique solution when the regularization parameter approaches zero, under specified monotonicity conditions.

In 1989, a conjecture was proposed regarding Fuchsian groups, stating that all their hyperbolic elements should have unique axes. This conjecture was validated for infinite Fuchsian groups of the first kind in 1990, for second kind groups in 2005, and for third kind groups in 2011. This paper will demonstrate that the conjecture also applies to the sixth type of Fuchsian groups, which have a topological disk as their space, and consists of surfaces with one cusp.

The ATLAS collaboration's search for the decay of right-handed theta quarks into a muon and b-quark is reported, utilizing a dataset of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions with an integrated luminosity of 36.1 inverse femtobarns from the CERN LHC in 2015. No evidence of a production and decay of theta quarks is found, and based on a 95% confidence level, upper limits on cross-sections and corresponding energy scales for new physics are established, ranging from 0.3 to 2.3 TeV for theta quark masses between 162 and 250 GeV.

Our research involves the synthesis of Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ through the reaction of PdS and P$_2$S$_5$ in a 1:1 ratio, and its DFT calculations. The Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ compound crystallizes in the monoclinic system with a space group C2/c, and an 8.5 angstroms $\times$ 9.5 angstroms $\times$ 5.5 angstroms lattice parameter. Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ maintains a superconducting state at high pressures, and its $T_{\rm C}$ is 4.5 Kelvin at 0.2 GPa. The compound exhibits a metal-semiconductor transition at 0.2 GPa and a phase transition at 2.0 GPa. The compound transforms into a metal at 2.0 GPa, and shows a metal-insulator transition at 4.0 GPa. The Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ compound exhibits a phase transition from a metal to an insulator at 4.0 GPa. The Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ compound shows a high sensitivity to pressure, and Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ is a promising superconducting material.

A new approach is developed to analyze the horizon's properties of a Schwarzschild black hole in the context of quantum mechanics. The horizon is divided into the fundamental and non-standard frameworks, and an infalling observer's experience is linked to their starting proper time upon being radiated out. The horizon's Rindler coordinates are used to calculate the fundamental framework's area and entropy. The effect of quantum mechanics is then applied to find the second quantized correction in entropy. The non-standard framework's Rindler coordinates are used to calculate the non-standard correction in entropy. The non-standard and quantum corrections are compared to those obtained from other black hole models. The non-standard correction in entropy is also expressed in terms of the starting proper time and is used to find the non-standard probability in the occurrence of the observer's radiating out time. The non-standard probability is compared to that obtained from the tunneling method. The non-standard probability in the occurrence of the radiating out time is compared to that obtained from the tunneling method.

Neural ODEs have gained popularity in approximating complex vector fields within high-dimensional spaces. This work explores the application of neural ODEs to inverse problems, specifically in the context of identifying unknown flows from noisy measurement data, and presents two novel methods: a first approach utilizes a neural ODE to predict the flow and subsequently reconstruct the vector field, and a second method directly learns the vector field from finite differences of the neural ODE's output. We examine the conditions under which these methods can produce consistent estimates of the true vector field and observe that the first approach is more resilient to noise but requires more data to achieve consistency, whereas the second method is more sensitive to noise but can learn the vector field with fewer samples.

We introduce the Object Memory Transformer (OMT), a novel architecture that 
enables the efficient navigation of 3D indoor scenes, primarily based on the
navigation between objects. OMT is built upon the Transformer framework and
incorporates the Transformer encoder to process visual and text-based input
information. A 3D object-centric decoder is developed to predict future actions
by analyzing the relationships between objects at different stages. OHTA's
performance is evaluated against top-performing baselines in the T-Map dataset
and consistently outperforms them in terms of successful navigation, particularly
in complex environments.

This research introduces a unified framework for the tuning of language models,
evaluating the impact of various parameters on the efficiency and performance of
the process. By examining the interplay of tuning methods, model types, dataset
compositions, and training duration, a comprehensive analysis is presented. The
study also investigates the application of LEMO models, which combine large and
efficient models to achieve superior results. Based on this framework, a set of
practical guidelines is derived and verified to facilitate the fine-tuning of
large language models.

Informal online groups that facilitate learning often lack clear guidance, causing participants to feel uncertain about their place within the community and what they're expected to achieve.  Participating in these groups without clear objectives can be intimidating, especially for newcomers, making it difficult for them to determine the level of participation that aligns with their goals.  This paper presents a conceptual framework that addresses this issue by reinterpreting the concept of legitimate peripheral participation in an informal learning setting.  The framework consists of four stages that reflect a newcomer's growing involvement in the community, thereby providing direction for participants at various stages of their participation.  The authors also introduce a process for identifying the various stages of participation, one that's adaptable to different community contexts.  This framework is being tested in an online community focused on informal learning, with initial results indicating its potential to enhance newcomers' participation and overall learning outcomes.

A novel approach to the transcorrelated method has been developed for use with the CASCI reference wave function, and successfully applied to large, extended systems with high accuracy, even in scenarios where traditional methods fail. The transcorrelated method has been found to maintain its accuracy even when dealing with complex, metallic systems that the random phase approximation often fails to handle, often producing more precise results than this traditional method. A key advantage of the transcorrelated method lies in its ability to achieve accurate results with significantly reduced computational costs, resulting in substantial time savings for complex calculations.

A mathematical model addressing location uncertainty uses a specific perturbation scheme to analyze a reaction-diffusion process affected by location errors. The standard method conserves mass but not the correct concentration in the long term due to location errors. By adjusting the initial data appropriately, we can maintain a balance between concentration and mass, thereby minimizing location errors over time. The proposed method is analyzed in one and two dimensions for finite difference and finite element numerical simulations. The results show that the balance of conservation laws is maintained, and numerical simulations demonstrate a significant reduction in location errors.

This research delves into the security implications of randomized big data storage and computation, exploring the potential of randomization to enhance both security and efficiency. By applying principles from information theory, we seek to establish a balance between computational complexity and information protection, minimizing the reliance on probabilistic techniques to guarantee security for all parties involved, including both authorized and unauthorized access to private data. We aim to derive a formula that represents the level of protection achieved through randomization, taking into account both the complexity of computations and the confidentiality of information. Furthermore, our approach will incorporate both public-key and cloud computing techniques to develop a comprehensive framework for understanding the security benefits of randomization in these environments.

To apply a policy trained in a simulated environment to a real-world setting, safety is paramount. However, ensuring safety in real-world environments is challenging due to unforeseen disturbances. To mitigate this, we propose SafeAPT, a risk-averse adaptation algorithm that uses an upper policy to monitor safety while navigating uncertainties. By utilizing an upper policy that minimizes risk, SafeAPT prevents the agent from deviating into hazardous states. We evaluate SafeAPT on a benchmark of Atari games and observe that it effectively recovers from failure rates comparable to human performance after only 20 minutes of reinforcement learning in the simulated environment.

The Fanaroff-Riley (FR) classification scheme separates FR I and FR II radio galaxies by their distinct morphological and jet features. This separation is primarily based on the influence of the surrounding intercluster medium. We have developed a new method to classify radio galaxies and studied how the FR classification relates to the environment. Our method involves measuring the Blandford-Kovner (BK) parameter from radio images and comparing it to the environment's beta value. When the BK/Beta ratio is above 0.5, the galaxy is classified as an FR I, below 0.5 a classification as an FR II, and between 0.5 and 1.5, it's considered a FR I/II mixed classification. Our analysis of 143 radio galaxies revealed a strong correlation between the BK/Beta ratio and the FR classification.
