However, our method also identified a subset of FR II galaxies with a BK/Beta ratio below 0.5, which suggests that the FR classification scheme may not be the only factor influencing jet morphology. This could be due to the environment's influence on the jet's interaction with the surrounding medium.

We introduce a novel approach to testing for the presence of parametric structural changes in models, such as AR processes, regression functions, without relying on certain assumptions like the error term's stationarity. This method can be applied to time series of any length and is not limited by the presence of out-of-sample observations as constraints in other methods do. This flexibility stems from our test's ability to validate the null hypothesis in the out-of-sample period, ensuring the test's validity in various scenarios. We demonstrate the test's power through Monte Carlo simulations and its application to real-world data in analyzing inflation rates.

This study examines the efficacy of multilingual models in processing social media content in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on both monolingual and multilingual models to evaluate their performance across different languages. We utilize a range of pre-trained models, ranging from straightforward word overlap models to sophisticated sequence-to-sequence models, to analyze and compare their outcomes, aiming to identify the most effective models and strategies for handling content from diverse linguistic backgrounds. The research reveals that, surprisingly, monolingual models often outperform their multilingual counterparts, highlighting the importance of considering the specific challenges and nuances of processing social media content in cross-lingual settings.

A novel approach to categorizing brain disorders based on functional neuroimaging data of the brain utilizes deep learning techniques. The approach integrates the limitations of generalised low-rank regularized matrix decomposition with deep learning architectures. The proposed model is based on GLRMD, which applies a hierarchical constraint to a linear combination of brain activity maps generated from fMRI data. This model is trained within a deep learning framework, with the goal of developing a system that can accurately classify brain disorders using the analysis of brain activity across multiple time points. The effectiveness of this approach was tested using a pre-existing dataset of brain activity maps from patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy individuals. The results demonstrate that GLRMD outperforms existing low-rank regularized models and traditional machine learning methods in terms of accuracy.

This paper investigates the control of the damped Euler-Bernoulli beam, a hybrid of Euler-Bernoulli and Kirchhoff-Birch systems, to achieve optimal control goals with finite time horizons in both free and forced scenarios. A comparison with related literature reveals improved convergence rates for energy dissipation, and the presence of Riccati equations in associated algebraic Riccati equations is explored.

A novel boundary treatment has been devised for high-order numerical schemes, such as the Spectral Difference (SD) method, by utilizing a complex function to achieve greater stability and accuracy. This new approach is compared to existing boundary treatments and provides analytical explanations, supported by numerical tests, which demonstrate its effectiveness. A boundary treatment modification for the Spectral Difference (SD) method has been derived using a specific function (1/((1n-x/nNn) + 1) to the power of α) and an extended form of the function (1/((1n-x/nNn)+(1/nP)(N-n/2)) to the power of α), resulting in improved results compared to the standard Spectral Difference (SD) method and the Spectral Discontinuity-Capture method.

Our study examines how varying the thickness of a silicon photonic crystal film impacts its optical absorption and transmission when paired with a dielectric layer on a silicon substrate. By using a dielectric layer to achieve time-reversal symmetry, we're able to counteract the inherent optical losses in the silicon that usually occur due to the material's complex refractive index. As a result, the optical absorption in the silicon film becomes less dependent on its thickness when it's thinner than the wavelength of light, and the dielectric layer's refractive index. Furthermore, the research shows that using this configuration can lead to increased transmission of up to 50% at thicker silicon film dimensions.

This study presents a topological credal library for a specific algebraic system.
The research defines how credal sets, a type of set-valued map that incorporates operations of union, intersection, and complement, relate to a topological space.
The existence of these operations was initially demonstrated by Baestaens and de Baets in 1996.
The work identifies an essential requirement for ensuring the credal library's operations result in compact topological spaces.
The research also introduces the concept of credal library of automata, a type of system that has been formalized here for the first time.
The authors develop a method to derive a credal library of automata from a credal library through a Galois connection.
The research also demonstrates that this method maintains compactness.

This study delves into the mathematical underpinnings of the widely used distance-based recommendation models. Initially, a comprehensive overview of the discrete Wasserstein distance is provided, along with its associated computational challenges. Building upon this foundation, two recommendation models are analyzed in detail, namely the collaborative filtering model utilizing the Wasserstein distance and the one-class SVM model, both of which are rigorously examined from a mathematical standpoint. In this work, we introduce an innovative linear time algorithm for computing the discrete Wasserstein distance, and demonstrate its utility in a recommendation system through a real-world dataset analysis, showcasing improved performance over one-class SVM.

We've developed a new quantum channel based on the quasi-ENM GAD model, and we've examined its non-Markovian behavior in comparison to the eternally non-Markovian property. Our results show that the GAD channel doesn't consistently exhibit non-Markovian behavior, but rather it depends on the initial state of the system. Furthermore, we explored the GAD channel's capacity for implementing quantum operations on pure states without any prior knowledge of the initial state, and we identified the conditions under which this is possible.

Current methods for evaluating machine learning models fall short in accurately
predicting performance on completely novel test data. We introduce CCRAL (Closed
Class Reconstruction of out-of-Domain data for out-of-Distribution data),
an effective approach that improves model generalization to unseen data.
CCRAL utilizes closed-class reconstruction, focusing on class-level
reconstruction metrics, and is compatible with any binary or multi-class model.
This method outperforms existing OOD detection methods in both simulated and
real-world data by being robust to data distribution shifts and noise. CCRAL is
also a complementary tool to enhance model training and evaluation, offering a
flexible framework for integrating additional features that can further boost
its performance.

The semantic mapping process involves merging a topological representation
of an environment with 3D spatial data to create a comprehensive model.
This model is crucial in robotics for various tasks such as autonomous
navigation and map sharing.
However, the current approaches to semantic mapping are limited by their
inability to accurately combine topological and spatial information.
Existing methods that use individual spatial and topological components
are not able to take advantage of the complementary strengths of both models.
Furthermore, the lack of a well-defined framework for integrating spatial
and topological data hinders the reproduction of results and slows down
robotics research.
In this paper, we introduce a novel framework called the Spatial-Topological
Discrete Representation Model that combines the two models in a single
environmental model.
This framework is based on a graph structure that is defined by the spatial
connectivity between environmental components and the semantic relationships
between these components.
The proposed model is designed to be easily extensible to various environments
and can be used to accurately represent environmental geometry and the
semantic labels of environmental components.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in a real-world
indoor robotic mapping scenario, where we use it to combine spatial and
topological data from a 2D lidar and a 3D SLAM system with a semantic
segmentation model.
The framework is also designed to be easily implemented using popular
robotics platforms and to be suitable for three-dimensional environments.

The Rikudo puzzle, a variant of the sliding puzzle found on mobile phones, can be solved in polynomial time when all odd numbers are grouped together and placed in an alternating checkered board starting with an odd number in the center.

In numerical analysis and machine learning, a range of optimization problems involving integral functions can be found, and a solution to one of these problems is the Kantorovich problem, also known as the Kantorovich transportation problem. To tackle this, a novel approach is proposed based on the Sinkhorn algorithm, and a new method is developed to efficiently solve the problem by first breaking it down into smaller sub-problems and then using a gradient descent method, such as the BFGS algorithm, to solve the resulting optimization problem. The approach is shown to be more efficient than the standard Sinkhorn's algorithm, especially when dealing with large-scale data sets. The new method is also applied to solve other related optimization problems, and a version of the algorithm is implemented in Python using the GPyLight package.

We have conducted a detailed study of gravitational lensing in two galaxy clusters, 
J0818-2613 and J1817+2729, using the COSMOS-100 and the Hubble Space Telescope's 
WFC3 G141 H-band images. By examining these images, we have been able to accurately 
determine the redshifts of the lensing galaxies, with deflectors J0818-2613 and J1817+2729 
having redshifts of 0.955 and 0.256 respectively. Furthermore, we have been able to 
measure the redshifts of the multiple images, with lensed source galaxies exhibiting 
redshifts of 2.84, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 2.51, 1.95, and 1.95. 
Utilizing the lens equation, we have been able to accurately predict the positions of the 
lensed images, with a maximum deviation of 0.5 arcseconds observed. By examining the 
multiple images, we have been able to determine their physical properties, including 
massive galaxy clusters, with mass estimates of 1.7x10^14 Msun and 1.5x10^14 Msun. 
Additionally, we have been able to determine the mass distribution of the lensing system

This article focuses on numerical solutions to a $q$-fractional differential equation's initial problem, utilizing the Caputo sense. By $q$-fractional differential equation, we refer to the first-order ordinary differential equation with $q$-fractional derivative. By $L^2 T^2$, we denote the anisotropic Sobolev space, and our objective is to derive $L^2 T^2$-valued $q$-fractional integral operator $I_t^q$ that maps $L^2 T^2$ to $L^2 T^2$. $I_t^q$ is then used to transform the $L^2 T^2$-valued $q$-fractional differential equation's initial problem into its integral problem, and by the difference method, we convert the $q$-fractional integral problem into the non-fractional one. By the difference method, we convert the $q$-fractional integral problem into the non-fractional one, and by the $L^2 T^2$-valued $Q$-integral operator, we convert the non-fractional problem into the $L^2 T^2$-valued $Q$-integral problem. The study of the phonon Hall effect in dielectric materials provides a valuable opportunity to investigate how narrow-bandgap systems respond to multicycle pulse excitation. By employing a multicycle pulse scheme, we can accurately determine the phonon Hall conductivity at the edge of a Brillouin zone in dielectric materials. Our calculations, which utilize the $\Gamma$-$X$ edge in silicon, reveal that magnetic fields can significantly enhance phonon Hall conductivity. Additionally, we have developed a method to calculate the effective Hall conductivity using multicycle pulse excitation, which can be applied to systems with larger bandgaps.

A novel nod and shuffle technique for wide-field imaging has been developed, which minimizes acquisition time even further than its two-dimensional counterpart. By shifting images through the telescope's focal plane and simultaneously oscillating in an orthogonal direction, the desired area can be covered within a single exposure without incurring inter-exposure delays. This method is particularly beneficial for surveys requiring fast data collection, such as those studying variable stars, transients, or extended objects. We have successfully implemented this technique on the 1m Jacob Hans Schmidt telescope at the South African Astronomical Observatory and present the results, which showcase the system's capabilities and feature high-quality, calibrated images of the Large Magellanic Cloud and extended Murchison Widefield Array images of the sky.

In 1976, Demjanov and Karlin introduced a two-variable inequality with significant implications in optimization and statistics. Our research builds upon this discovery by generalizing it to matrix-based inequalities and explores their significance in matrix theory. We derive multiple findings, including the establishment of a p-Hyers-Ulam stability and a matrix version of the inequality that is equivalent to hyperbolic inequality conditions, where the inequality's lower bound is adjusted to matrix norms. We also uncover novel inequalities tied to the maximum row sum, maximum column sum, and maximum absolute value row sum of a matrix. Lastly, we illustrate these concepts through practical applications in supply chain management.

We examine the average null energy condition along the event horizon of a spherical black hole that forms and disappears in a specific space-time context. First, we investigate this condition in a static state and find that it's supported by various matter configurations that conform to specific fundamental principles. Next, we study the event of black hole formation within an expanding universe and observe that the average null energy condition is satisfied at the moment of formation. Interestingly, we find that this condition is violated during the evaporation process. A similar outcome is observed when the black hole is formed in a space with specific properties. Finally, we investigate how the average null energy condition evolves along the event horizon during a black hole's formation and evaporation in a space with certain properties, and discover that it first appears positive, then becomes negative as the evaporation progresses. Our research is significant because it sheds light on the average null energy condition while also revealing the intriguing behavior of black hole evaporation.

In a four-dimensional Conformal Field Theory, we analyze the impact of a small, irrelevant operator on the trace anomaly within a framework of heat kernel expansion, demonstrating that the influence is entirely contained in two heat kernel parameters. Specifically, when the irrelevant operator is either a c-number or a non-c-number, we have found that the heat kernel parameters exhibit distinct behavior, with one parameter exhibiting a simple scaling in the irrelevant operator's dimension while the second follows a more complex pattern. Importantly, our results show that the conventional trace anomaly is restored when the irrelevant operator vanishes, and the heat kernel parameters return to their well-known Tidrow formulas.

The cybersecurity testbeds in the Industrial Control Systems (ICS) community have been instrumental in promoting the development of secure products and well-coordinated responses to emerging threats. However, the rapid evolution of ICS cybersecurity demands continuous assessment and improvement of these testbeds to keep pace with these developments. This paper proposes a maturity model to assess the progress and provide guidance for improving ICS cybersecurity through the testbeds. By focusing on specific aspects of control systems and their interaction with users, the model aims to facilitate the understanding of how testbeds are affected. It also aims to provide practical advice for using the model at various points in its construction.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, accurately estimating the value function is crucial. Current methods, like GAE off-policy estimation, have limitations, especially in high-dimensional settings where they struggle to learn. A new approach, the greedy-based value representation (GVR), addresses these issues. GVR leverages the greedy policy to generate actions for any given state, allowing for the creation of a supervised learning dataset. By comparing GVR with GAE in a challenging MARL task, it became apparent that GVR learns significantly faster and outperforms GAE in terms of task completion.

We introduce StereoSet, a large, open-source, and diverse dataset for assessing and studying stereotypical biases in language. This dataset comprises 4,700 examples across four areas: physical appearance, mental health, racial identity, and gender identity. Each example is coupled with four statements: a neutral statement and three stereotypical representations of a particular individual. We also provide human annotations evaluating the degree of stereotypical bias in language for these statements. We conducted an analysis of StereoSet to explore the presence of biases in language and discovered that the extent and direction of biases differ significantly across domains and categories. We then used StereoSet to train supervised models capable of identifying and quantifying stereotypical biases in language with high accuracy, outperforming both unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches. We also demonstrate that these models can be applied to detect and quantify biases in other languages more effectively than previous methods.

In this study, we develop a learning method to determine optimal tilt update policies within a distributed network of sensors that collaborate to identify and track changes in sensor readings using a distributed optimization algorithm. Our goal is to minimize the combined tracking error, considering various system parameters, such as measurement accuracy, communication constraints, and number of collaborating sensors. To achieve this, we employ the Contextual Multi-Armed-Bandit framework to learn the best update policy without requiring real-world data, thereby reducing the need for iterative simulations. Our approach significantly reduces learning time, with experimental results validating its effectiveness by surpassing the performance of traditional learning methods.

The LHCb experiment has made precise calculations based on the $B_s^0 \to D_s^{\pm} D_s^\mp/\bar{D_s}^\mp D_s^{\mp}$ decays, utilizing the entire dataset collected from Run 1 and Run 2. These findings have led to improved estimates of $\gamma$ and the branching ratios for various $B$ decays. The CKM angle $\gamma$ has a 95.5% confidence interval ranging between 48.4° and 93.3°. The experiment has also yielded the first significant measurement of the ratio of decay rates for $B_s^0 \to D_s^+ D_s^-$ and $B_s^0 \to D_s^- D_s^+$, as well as the branching ratio of $B^0 \to D_s^- D^0$.

Our research demonstrates the applicability of the complex Euclidean space concept to the study of convex bodies, revealing connections between complex symmetry, central sections, and projections. We've found that the symmetry of a three-dimensional convex body is characterized by the properties of its central sections when considering the Euclidean norm, whereas its symmetry in the hyperbolic norm is encoded in the properties of its essential sections. Moreover, we've established that the complex symmetry of a body equals the symmetry of its Minkowski auto-product decomposition's least component.

The collection and monetization of personal data has become a lucrative business, but it remains unclear how individuals perceive the commercial exchange of their data. Our research involves a survey where real participants sell their personal data in a market, and the data is analyzed using an auction model. Our findings, which are based on actual human subjects, reveal that as the number of participants selling their data in an auction increases, the prices they assign to their personal data do not decrease in a predictable manner. In fact, there are instances where personal data that is analytically distinct is assigned the same price by the sellers. These observations challenge existing market theories and highlight the need for a new framework to understand how personal data is valued in a market setting.

FTN signaling simplifies detection complexity but introduces increased
channel estimation intricacy, which is further exacerbated by its adaptive
nature. To mitigate this, we suggest a novel deep learning-based approach,
combining both long-term and short-term channel prediction capabilities. To
achieve this, two distinct deep neural networks are employed: one for generating
the initial short-term prediction functions, which are then used to refine the
short-term prediction for the current time step, resulting in the generation of
an updated prediction function. Through our method, the absolute error in
estimating channel phase and magnitude is reduced to around $0.0004$ and
$0.0008$ radian, and $10^{-4}$ respectively at a $200\times 10^{-6}$ symbol
error rate. Furthermore, the proposed approach demonstrates improved
performance in adaptive channel prediction compared to a conventional LMS
methodology.

In the realm of effect algebras, the primary focus lies within complete atomic effect algebras, which are subsets of certain lattice effect algebras. This paper delves into the properties of the Frink and order topologies within these mathematical structures, with a particular emphasis on their equivalence for specific distributive lattice effect algebras. Furthermore, the study provides conditions under which the category of complete atomic effect algebras with continuous homomorphisms would form a topological category.

This work presents SaliencyMix, a straightforward technique that improves the accuracy of object detection (OD) models by modifying the training data to reflect human attention. SaliencyMix introduces a novel data augmentation method that incorporates salient information from additional external sources, enhancing the quality of the training dataset. By leveraging saliency maps from external sources, SaliencyMix becomes a relevant data augmentation technique. Our experiments demonstrate that SaliencyMix significantly improves model performance, yielding up to 7% mAP gains, and can be combined with other data augmentation methods without reducing their effectiveness.

In 1988, Vershik and Kerov created a complete categorization of the indecomposable properties of positive tracers on infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebras in the setting of finite groups. We build on the foundational work of Laver to demonstrate that the same classification can be achieved using only lambda-terms and simple combinations of numbers.

We explore the alignment parameter, $\eta$, for a modified gravity theory known as $f(R)$, which influences the relationship between a galaxy's intrinsic shape and the large-scale alignment of surrounding galaxies. Using a cosmological simulation, we find that the alignment between galaxies is primarily driven by gravity and not by dark matter, with significant correlations observed at specific angular scales. Specifically, at $0.3-0.6$ degrees, $\eta$ is found to be approximately $0.04-0.05$, with the alignment parameter varying based on galaxy luminosity. Our results also indicate that the alignment parameter is more sensitive to the growth rate of structures than to the intrinsic shape of galaxies. By utilizing the observed alignment parameter $\eta$, we estimate the dark matter fraction in a galaxy sample to be approximately $0.78$.

Soft, flexible particle systems can exhibit long-term memory characteristics that stem from the rearrangement dynamics of particles during loading, influencing subsequent response patterns. The effects of reversal, where the direction of loading is reversed, can provide insight into the underlying mechanisms responsible for non-hysteretic, secondary-memory driven, or stress relaxation-like behavior. In this study, we investigate a soft, flexible particle system subjected to cyclic loading via particle image velocimetry (PIV) and measure stress by calculating the resistance to particle deformation through resistance torque. The results show that the arrangement of particles and their rearrangement are correlated, with a notable shift in particle flow from localized to global patterns as the number of cycles increases. The system's memory, as measured by changes in stress over cycles, exhibits a complex relationship with its rearrangement patterns, which evolve in response to strain reversal, leading to a reduction in the number of rearrangement events and a shift towards a more localized flow pattern.

The phase change of gold nanoparticles, studied using in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction, was observed to be influenced by the thermal treatment of their 110 plane. The nanoparticles' structure was found stable at temperatures up to 550°C for particles measuring 3 nm and up to 120°C for larger 10 nm and 12 nm particles. The melting process in the 3 nm particle occurred smoothly over 200°C, whereas it was a sharp transition for the 10 nm and 12 nm particles. The temperature of the phase change was determined to be dependent on particle size with the values 1420°C, 714°C, and 680°C for the 3 nm, 10 nm, and 12 nm particles respectively.

We initially tackle a generalized quasi-linear elliptic boundary value problem, tailored to a specific open domain $\Omega$ within an $n$-dimensional space, $n \ge 3$. By slightly relaxing the standard requirement for differentiability in the coefficients $A$, we are able to extend the scope of applicable coefficients. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence and distinctiveness of a solution for this generalized problem, utilizing this as a stepping stone to establish the existence of a solution for a generalized quasilinear elliptic obstacle problem, a problem that previously lacked a proof of existence.

In a five-dimensional model with a warped, circular space-time (5D RS-I), we investigate the issue of horizontal anomalies in the Standard Model by incorporating two new, massless fields with non-zero $U(1)_{L_i-L_j}$ charges. The 5D RS-I space is separated into two regions: a highly warped section near the boundary and a less warped section closer to the AdS edge. We propose that the first, warped region is connected to the Standard Model through a5D brane, while the second, less warped section contains quarks and a lepton along with their corresponding anti-particles, which are localized in distinct regions. This set-up allows for a relationship between quarks and anti-leptons that resolves both the $U(1)_{L_i-L_j}$ and $U(1)_{B-L}$ horizontal anomalies, without affecting the Standard Model's gauge anomalies, and also addresses the proton's stability without introducing any new, massless particles.

Utilizing the multi-variable fermionic technique coupled with the Dobinsky-type formula allowed us to derive identities for (h; q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials, where the identities encompassed a range of special polynomials and numbers, including fermionic numbers, (h; q)-Daehee numbers, (q-1; q)n-Bernoulli numbers and polynomials, as well as their corresponding transformations.

This study explores the application of reinforcement learning to tackle non-stationary challenges in estimating the average reward with a discrete-time, finite-state, and finite-action model that changes over time according to an unknown distribution. We have devised two algorithms: the first uses online prediction and the second leverages the online estimate from both the prediction and control approaches. We have established that these algorithms can accurately estimate the average reward with high probability, achieving a maximum error within two associated change detection rates. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the proposed algorithms can learn and adapt to the non-stationary environment by rapidly estimating the change detection rates.

This letter introduces a causal inference method for evaluating paired observations, enabling the calculation of confidence intervals (CIs) even when data is missing. For paired data, traditional confidence intervals using a t-test or permutation tests may not be feasible due to the presence of missing data, which complicates inference on causal parameters. This letter addresses this challenge by proposing a hybrid inference method, which combines parametric and non-parametric approaches to construct confidence intervals for the causal odds ratio (COR) in paired data. This hybrid method first estimates the conditional probability of missing data using a parametric model and calculates a maximum likelihood estimate. Subsequently, the method utilizes permutation tests to obtain non-parametric CIs. When data is nearly balanced, the parametric estimate is used to adjust the permutation CIs. In cases where the data imbalance persists, the correlation between observed and missing data is estimated using a non-parametric approach and applied to refine the permutation CIs. Simulation studies have validated the method's performance, which was also successfully demonstrated on a real-world dataset from a recent study published in JAMA.

Recent research has shown that using invertible layers in autoencoder construction leads to improved performance in both log-likelihood and sample quality, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data.  While previous studies have demonstrated the potential of invertible layers, the main challenge remains in their practical implementation, as their analytical Jacobian can only handle independent inputs.  To overcome this limitation, the current research focuses on incorporating invertible layers into a deep generative model, allowing for the generation of high-quality images with optimal entropy.  By combining invertible layers with standard building blocks, the proposed model achieves an improved performance of 2.05 bits per pixel in log-likelihood and 0.16 in log likelihood gradient entropy on the CIFAR10 dataset, while also providing a computationally stable training process.

This research paper outlines our participation in the 2018 Data Visualization Competition, highlighting our advanced visualization system that utilizes cloud-based analytics and high-resolution geospatial data. The resulting visualizations empower users to comprehensively understand the process of analyzing smart city data. Through an in-depth case study, we examine the challenges we encountered, highlight the success factors behind our leading placement, and explore future developments and drawbacks of our created system.

In recent years, hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods have gained significant attention due to their high-order accuracy and ability to be implemented with fewer degrees of freedom. However, the linear systems resulting from these methods are challenging to solve efficiently. This study focuses on the black-box geometric multigrid preconditioning technique for these systems, which has not been previously explored in the literature. By generating an optimal coarse-scale matrix from the discontinuous Galerkin matrix and an efficient interpolation operator between grids, the method improves the efficiency of solving the linear system. The performance of this method is evaluated using a variety of test problems with different mesh sizes and grid distributions, yielding a significant reduction in computational costs.

To draw causal conclusions, we must assess how robust they are to uncertainties in background knowledge. When certain data is missing, it's not possible to directly evaluate the robustness. Our research offers a novel approach to quantifying the robustness of causal inferences when some of the underlying probabilities are unknown. By converting the inference into a Bayesian model, we can calculate the model's posterior, then use the E-value to obtain a probability measure that reflects our uncertainty in the posterior conclusion based on the model's uncertainty in the posterior parameters. By examining the E-value, we can identify the extent to which our causal conclusions remain robust. When data is abundant, the E-value approaches zero, signifying a high level of robustness. Conversely, a high E-value indicates a low level of robustness. We demonstrate this methodology using an analysis of the risk factors for type 2 diabetes.

In studies involving crossover designs with a limited number of subjects, data loss can be quite substantial, causing significant issues in deriving reliable estimates of treatment effects. To tackle this problem, we've developed a Bayesian approach to handle missing data and provide reliable estimates of treatment effects in crossover designs. This method, which relies on a data augmentation technique, utilizes a locally dependent sequence model to accurately model the missing data process. Additionally, our approach offers a simple method to incorporate prior knowledge regarding the number of subjects and effectively quantify the uncertainty associated with the number of subjects required for accurate inference. Through a comprehensive simulation study, we've demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in handling missing data and accurately capturing uncertainty. Furthermore, our method has been successfully applied to a real-world dataset, obtained from a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a new treatment in reducing COVID-19 transmission.

The underlying structure of a category's nerve, a topological category, is analyzed through $A_n$ structures, which have distinct meanings depending on the value of n, including group actions and the more general concept of a presheaf. This analysis is applied to the fundamental groupoid of a category's nerve, and specific cases concerning categories built from the fundamental groupoids of topological spaces are examined.

A novel DRAM PUF, known as DRAM-PUF, utilizes the inherent properties of DRAM cells to generate unpredictable readouts, making it an attractive solution for security applications. To evaluate the performance of this PUF, we developed a reliable read mechanism that overcame issues related to DRAM cell degradation caused by high-speed reads. Our solution involves identifying optimal read parameters and utilizing a circuit-level cache to efficiently process high-speed reads. As a result, we successfully created a high-speed DRAM PUF that maintains robust performance even with diverse supply voltages and varying operating temperatures. Our approach yields an average survival rate of 85.6% at 1.2V and 90°C, and 78.2% at 1.2V and -10°C, with an average delay of 0.9 ns. To further assess the PUF's reliability, we developed a novel method to detect and remove unreliable chips, yielding an average delay of 0.7 ns and a survival rate of 95.6% at 1.2V and -10°C, with only 1.2% of chips affected. Our proposed DRAM PUF exhibits superior performance, with a high success rate of 94.4%, with an average delay of 0.7 ns and 1.2% unclonable chips, outperforming existing DRAM PUFs.

Functionally programming the composition and management of virtualized network resources is becoming increasingly crucial, but current programming languages are often too restrictive in their use of predefined functions, making it difficult to create complex control flow structures. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed the P4 programmable switch and the Binary Neural Network Interpreter (BNII), an advanced programming language that allows users to create custom control flow branches. By leveraging the unique architecture of the BNNI switch, it's now possible to create a new control flow structure using existing components, rather than being limited by predefined functions. This flexibility is further enhanced by integrating the BNNI switch with other network components, enabling the creation of an adaptable control flow pipeline that can be easily reconfigured through retraining of the switch's neural network.

We propose a novel framework for evaluating quantum gate performance, which leverages logical error rates to gauge the efficiency of quantum processing. This framework is founded on a toric code, with its non-Clifford gate implementation based on a stabilizer error correcting code. The code's surface code, enhanced through code concatenation with toric codes, enables the assessment of higher-order logical error rates. Consequently, the method facilitates the evaluation of gate performance on various platforms utilizing surface codes, and offers a more precise means of estimating quantum computing's overall performance. This framework is then applied to compare the effectiveness of different gate technologies, including n-qubit gate sets employed in randomized benchmarking studies for ion, superconducting, and semiconducting quantum platforms. The results of our analysis reveal that the gate sets of ion and superconducting systems have comparable performance capabilities, and surpass that of semiconducting quantum processing by significant margins.

The growing demand for high-performance computing has led to increased adoption of computing clusters, necessitating innovative solutions to optimize job execution.  This study introduces the Universal Worker System (UWS), a distributed worker framework that enables parallel execution of tasks within computing clusters.  By utilizing message passing and user-defined functions, UWS allows for flexible task customization and worker initialization.  Once a computing node is powered on, it automatically becomes a UWS worker, ready to receive and process tasks.  UWS's master node tracks available workers, and it can be bypassed by workers, allowing for direct task submissions and decoupling from the master component.  UWS supports multiple task types, including those with non-deterministic output and those requiring dynamic resource allocation during execution, through a self-adjusting worker count.  By leveraging the master's knowledge of the computing cluster's structure, UWS can optimize task placement and resource allocation, and it can be easily extended to accommodate custom job types.  UWS has been successfully deployed on various supercomputers, including Blue Waters, IBM PowerEdge, and Intel XeonPhi, and it has been utilized in a variety of applications, such as high-performance computing, machine learning, and real-time data processing.

The wireless communications and networking field is witnessing accelerated growth, driven by multiple interconnected factors. The rapid advancement is attributed to the integration of cutting-edge technologies like artificial intelligence, machine learning, and wireless sensing. However, the traditional research assessment methods, based on author keynotes and reputation, fail to account for collaborative efforts and credit individual authors fairly. To bridge this gap, a new approach is proposed to recognize the contributions of each author to specific studies, enabling a more comprehensive and accurate credit distribution. To achieve this, a blockchain-based system is proposed to record research credits, enabling the establishment of a fair and equitable credit system. The proposed system is applied to the IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications (TWC) to demonstrate its effectiveness in assigning credits, and its impact is examined through the lenses of research assessment methods and the distribution of credits among authors. The proposed system is also expected to facilitate blockchain-empowered learning in future wireless networks.

The presence of O2 and CH4 in the atmospheres of terrestrial exoplanets allows for the determination of their atmospheric conditions. Our research on atmospheric chemistry on planets with thick atmospheres reveals that these molecules are produced in significant quantities, even when the atmosphere is heavily influenced by 3-bar pressure, high temperatures, and strong water vapor presence. Our results show a strong correlation between O2 levels and planetary temperature, as well as an inverse correlation between O2 levels and CH4 levels. However, we also found that these correlations weaken under low-pressure conditions, as well as when there is a strong water vapor presence. Our study also found that, with the presence of water, the amount of O2 produced in the atmosphere is largely influenced by the amount of water present, rather than the amount of organic carbon present.

The phenomenon of surface currents in one-dimensional systems has garnered significant attention, particularly due to their unique behavior in systems of both bosonic and fermionic nature. A comprehensive study of surface currents in one-dimensional systems, including systems with a finite number of sites, has been conducted. The research reveals that the presence of these currents in finite systems is a result of unphysical, random numbers used to populate the lowest energy band. A novel approach to eliminating these random currents has been proposed, and the results have been applied to actual quantum systems, specifically the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. The findings suggest that the surface currents can be removed by applying specific phase shifts to specific sites. The results of this research are expected to contribute to the understanding and control of surface currents in one-dimensional systems, particularly in systems with a finite number of sites.

Our research focuses on enhancing multilingual neural machine translation capabilities by adapting to a specific domain within the medical context. The study evaluates the effectiveness of two approaches - using a single multilingual model for translation and using a specialized model for each language and domain, dubbed TMTrans. The latter method, TMTrans, consists of two training methods: training a language pair and using a semi-supervised approach that incorporates unseen data in training. The results show that TMTrans significantly outperforms a standard model in the medical context and even surpasses a specially trained English medical translator in terms of quality. Notably, we observed a substantial reduction in the cost of creating medical translation datasets through TMTrans.

This study examines the creation and propagation of solitary and shock waves within a dusty plasma system consisting of warm ions, superthermal electrons, and both positive and negative dust particles.  Using the reductive perturbation method, a nonlinear Schrödinger equation was derived for the perturbation variables, and its properties were subsequently analyzed.  It was found that the ion fluid temperature, superthermal electron parameter, and the charge of dust particles significantly influence the conditions necessary for the formation and propagation of solitary and shock waves.  Furthermore, our results indicate that for a specific range of electron parameter values, the conditions required for the formation of shock waves are more stringent than those necessary for solitary waves.

This study introduces a contrastive context prediction (CCP) task for developing universal sentence embeddings in multilingual environments. CCP involves learning from pairs of sentences with varied context representations, which can be manipulated through factors like language and word order. In contrast to existing techniques, CCP doesn't rely on language identification or advanced NLP tools. Our findings indicate that CCP outperforms other methods in achieving generalization across languages, particularly when paired with supervised fine-tuning. Furthermore, CCP achieves competitive results in zero-shot cross-lingual and zero-shot multilingual transfer learning tasks, even surpassing monolingual pre-training methods like WLM and DLM.

In real-world applications, different modalities exhibit varying data availability and processing speeds. While faster modalities such as images are typically rich in detailed information, slower modalities like speech are often more informative over time. To address this, we introduce the Prototypical Modality Rebalance (PMR) approach, which enables a multimodal learner to adjust the effective representation of the slower modality by utilizing prototypical samples from the more rapid modality. These samples are selected based on their similarity to the current input and used to rebalance the model's hidden state. The process of selecting and incorporating these samples enhances the model's ability to capture long-term contextual information and accurately classify words, even with limited information available. Experimental results on speech-based classification tasks confirm that PMR significantly improves the model's performance and achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy in a speech-based visual-voice recognition task.

The standard kinetic equation is derived from the one-particle Wigner function.
However, when applied to kinetic theory, this equation assumes a uniform particle
density, which is unrealistic in realistic physical scenarios. This paper argues
that when particle density diverges is taken into account, kinetic equations for
massless fermions become infinitely deep, requiring a specific scaling of the
Wigner function to remain well-behained. A proposed solution involves a phase
shift that can be significant for small momenta and large densities. This effect
was overlooked in previous works on kinetic theory, including a recent model for
quark-gluon plasma in strong coupling, where a corresponding correction is
applied.

In the context of command and control systems, we evaluate the effectiveness of two types of models: CNN and CNN+(CNN+TT-DNN). These models were trained using the MCC-DARPA dataset, specifically the "grandma" and 'aircraft carrier' scenarios. Our findings show that the CNN+(TT-DNN) model performs better in terms of command recognition accuracy, but is less efficient due to its larger parameter count. In contrast, CNN+(CNN+TT-DNN) with larger parameters outperformed CNN with smaller parameters.

We propose an approach to modify a deterministic system driven by external forces, 
where a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian evolution is allowed. Our method focuses on 
transforming the initial non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into a Hermitian form, 
enabling the use of the time-dependent perturbation theory. As an example, 
we examine a periodically driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain and find that a 
weak, low-frequency external force can induce a topological transition even at 
high driving frequencies.

A new method to boost the efficiency of plasmonic solar cells is presented using a technique that controls light concentration and absorption. By optimizing the design of these cells and using specific materials with a wavelength of 900 nanometers, we achieved a conversion efficiency of 24.2 percent with aluminum nanoparticles, which nearly matches the maximum efficiency of gold nanoparticles in similar conditions. Our approach also allows for the creation of highly efficient solar cells using cost-effective materials with a wavelength that minimizes heat emission and energy loss due to biological interactions.

The combination of an algebra of binary relations and linear-time modal dynamic logic provides a suitable framework for analyzing and modeling various computational processes. This study examines the theoretical foundations of such a framework, incorporating a relation algebra and a modal logic. The authors establish a set of foundational axioms for these logical structures, similar to those proposed by Goldblatt, and subsequently derive multiple models including mathematical semigroups, a lattice of subsets, and the Stone algebra of closed subspaces. Additionally, the authors discuss general properties inherent in the combined logic system.

Deep learning models have significantly benefited from the development of the tensor decomposition-based approach, known as tensor train, which can efficiently decompose high-dimensional data. However, the current model-oriented hardware design often struggles with performance and power consumption. This work presents a novel hardware model, FDHT-LSTM, which leverages the tensor decomposition FDHT algorithm to process tensor trains in parallel, minimizing the need for general-purpose processing. The proposed design is highly scalable, capable of handling three-dimensional tensor trains. The simulation results demonstrate that FDHT-LSTM outperforms traditional model-oriented hardware in terms of throughput, with a significant reduction in energy consumption for large-scale tensors by a factor of 7.5. Moreover, FDHT-LSTM boasts a substantial 1024-fold improvement in throughput compared to traditional model-oriented hardware from a computational perspective.

This paper presents a secure data transmission protocol for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) using ground-based systems. The protocol is based on a message exchange framework, similar to the UAV network (MAVLink), and incorporates a data encryption mechanism for MAVLink messages and related control commands using various cryptographic algorithms. The study assesses the performance of the encryption methods, including decryption speed and error rates, and identifies AES-128 as the most efficient option for encrypting MAVLink messages and control commands.

The complexity of network behavior stems from the interactions of individual nodes and their connections, making it challenging to accurately represent network performance using traditional simulation methods. These approaches often rely on intricate models that replicate network details, limiting their application in practical scenarios. To address this issue, we present a simplified emulation model that focuses on end-to-end properties, allowing us to separate the impact of various network characteristics and settings on application performance. By utilizing this model, we can determine the optimal settings that minimize delays in network synchronization while ensuring accurate estimation, thus making it feasible to conduct reliable emulations of large-scale networks despite the lack of access to real-time network data.

A novel geometric interpretation has been developed for the Newman-Penrose mapping, expressed as the intersection of two twistor distributions at a null geodesic. The invariance properties of this mapping can be geometrically explained from the twistor perspective, unlike the traditional representation which retains its form under linear transformations of the Newman-Penrose adapted coordinates. The new twistorial view also offers a straightforward method to compute the Weyl tensor's residues from a single asymptotic condition. The twistorial representation of the Newman-Penrose mapping has further implications for its application in asymptotic geometry and the Newman-Penrose mapping.

The Muon Scuola, an early prototype of a cosmic ray muon telescope, was developed to serve as a educational tool for science education in Italy's primary schools. This prototype, an unshielded scintillator detector, has the potential to be easily replicated and installed in multiple locations worldwide, making it an ideal educational and research resource due to its sensitivity. Its versatility also extends to a range of scientific applications, including the exploration of cultural heritage sites and complex infrastructure environments like data storage facilities and scientific research laboratories.

This research introduces PEGLL, an advanced GLL parsing technique, which builds upon the foundational work of GLL by Harrison. PEGLL parsing is distinguished by its ability to handle arbitrary context-free grammars, in contrast to traditional GLL parsing, which is often limited to LL(1)-formulas. PEGLL's key characteristics include: (i) support for arbitrary context-free grammars; (ii) single-table parsing; (iii) a deterministic parsing process; (iv) capability to handle epsilon transitions. The authors formally describe PEGLL parsing and provide a formal proof of its correctness. Furthermore, they outline a set of essential conditions that must be satisfied by the GLL parser, and provide a detailed example that showcases the capabilities of PEGLL parsing. The authors also discuss the relationship between PEGLL and GLL, and provide a detailed example that highlights the limitations of GLL parsing.

A quantum particle in an empty space faces a fundamental challenge when trying to emit radiation, and this challenge is a direct result of the thermodynamic principle that heat cannot travel faster than light.  Even with no restrictions, the theoretical possibility of such radiation does not result in an infinite energy output; however, the transmission of heat information faster than light than heat would violate causality, a violation that would occur instantaneously.  Our research has found that this radiation phenomenon is not feasible because it would be impossible at high temperatures, where the theoretical laws of thermodynamics would be broken.  Our findings are based on the analysis of the quantum process of emitting a single photon, a process that can be described by a mathematical formula.  The analysis involves calculating the rate of radiation, a process that depends on the temperature and is typically measured in units of energy per unit mass per unit time.  The calculated rate of radiation is zero at absolute zero temperatures, increases at a constant temperature, and is impossible at high temperatures, where the theoretical laws of thermodynamics would be broken.  Our findings are based on the analysis of the quantum process and the application of the Hegerfeldt inequality, a mathematical rule that describes the relationship between the properties of the system, the speed of light, and the rate of emission.

To grasp language, we need to recognize unexpected words in sentences, but predicting predictable words using one or two words at a time is insufficient for comprehending the big picture. This study shows that considering more context is crucial for grasping word predictability, whether we're looking at typical linguistic patterns or the individual meanings of words. Additionally, we found that using longer contexts improves our ability to predict word predictability, aligning with recent findings on other language processing tasks.

In this research, we develop a two-stage training method for 3D estimation models, where the first stage involves learning a comprehensive database of standard object poses, and the second stage involves utilizing a small dataset of real-world objects to refine the model. By doing so, we aim to create a robust 6D RANSAC-based estimator for use in applications where a large dataset of real-world objects is typically used to train the 3D estimation model. Our results demonstrate that this two-stage approach enables the 3D estimation model to achieve the same level of accuracy as a model trained on a large dataset of real-world objects, using a significantly smaller dataset. Our analysis also reveals that this approach leads to improved robustness against extreme outliers and enhanced 3D estimation accuracy.

We investigate the influence of intrinsic spin-orbit coupling on inter-dot gate-controlled coupling in InSb nanowire quantum dots, particularly in the double-dot configuration. Our results show that the application of magnetic fields leads to a substantial reduction in the coupling strength, with the fields causing a synchronized change in the spin-orbit splitting of each dot. Furthermore, specific field orientations exhibit field-dependent gate voltages that fine-tune the spin-orbit interaction, thereby adjusting the coupling strength. Notably, the fields enable the optimization of the coupling to favor either parallel or antiparallel spin alignments without compromising the device's charge control.

The traditional two-dimensional (2D) model used to study the solar wind is limited due to its inability to accurately account for the effects of pitch-angle scattering. This paper presents a new 3D model that includes the scattering process and allows for comparison with an alternative 3D model. By simulating the solar wind in a simplified 3D box, the new model replicates the results of the 2D model, but with the added feature of pitch-angle scattering. This comparison reveals that including the scattering process significantly alters the energy distribution of the particles. Furthermore, the new model provides a more accurate description of the solar wind, with improved agreement with in-situ measurements.

The Higgs diphoton decay rate measurement serves as a crucial test for extended scalar sectors that could potentially affect the Higgsstrahlung process, which includes the production of a W or Z boson in conjunction with a Higgs boson. Utilizing data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2016, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.4 fb$^{-1}$, the production of a W boson in conjunction with a Higgs boson was studied. This study focused on events characterized by the presence of a W boson decaying into a lepton and a neutrino, and a Higgs boson decaying into a photon and a photon pair. A comparison of the observed events with the standard model predictions revealed a good match. As a result, constraints were established on the kinetic misalignment and mass parameter of a two-Higgs-doublet model.
This research delves into numerical properties of the joint numerical radius and its utilization in resolvent inequalities and best approximation.

The recent PATE framework has gained popularity for its innovative approach to protecting data privacy in machine learning models.  This approach has been found to significantly enhance the generalizability of models trained on reduced datasets.  Our study compares PATE with the widely used DP-SGD framework.  Our findings reveal that PATE surpasses DP-SGD in terms of privacy protection, but DP-SGD outperforms PATE in terms of model accuracy.  A notable exception was observed in credit risk and loan evaluation scenarios, where PATE excelled over DP-SGD.  Our results also indicate that combining these frameworks can lead to improved outcomes, with the integration of DP-SGD and PATE yielding better privacy protection and enhanced model performance.  These findings are based on our experiments with prominent financial datasets, including Loan25k and Bank Loan, which provide valuable insights into applying these frameworks to financial machine learning models.

The general Wold type decomposition is established for multivariate second-order random distribution fields, with the corresponding spectral matrix distribution of the difference being absolutely continuous. It's found that a stationary random distribution field is obtained from this decomposition if the mean of the filtered process is zero. This process is then defined as the orthogonal projection of the random distribution field onto the stationary component, and the randomness of the remaining difference is investigated. Moreover, a specific class of random distribution fields, characterized by their finite energy, undergo a mean-square transformation, resulting in a stationary distribution field, and the original random distribution is reconstructed from its stationary component and the transformed random field.

The relationship between a laser beam and a gas mixture containing dust or impurities is investigated, with a focus on how these elements interact and influence one another. Ignition characteristics of the gas mixture are analyzed through the spectrum of light emitted, and a mathematical relationship describing this emission is derived. Furthermore, a condition is established to gauge the laser's energy level, and numerical data is provided to demonstrate the accuracy of this approach.

A new boundary-based segmentation method, called BASeg, has been developed to tackle the challenges in medical imaging. The existing fully convolutional networks often struggle with incomplete information, object boundaries, and missing data, resulting in inaccurate predictions. To overcome these issues, BASeg has been designed with a boundary-aware network that incorporates spatial and boundary information. The effectiveness of BASeg has been evaluated using various medical image segmentation tasks, including multi-organ segmentation, cardiac structure segmentation from 3D echocardiography, and tumor segmentation from complex imaging data. The results demonstrate BASeg's ability to accurately segment objects with missing data, missing boundaries, and missing voxels, achieving state-of-the-art performance in these challenging tasks. The code for BASeg will be publicly available on GitHub under the terms of the Apache 2.0 license.

The Driver Messenger System is a communication system designed to enhance safety by enabling vehicles to notify each other of impending lane changes, thereby reducing the risk of collisions. As vehicles approach a potential collision point, they activate the system, transmitting a pre-saved lane change plan to nearby vehicles. These systems have been implemented in Japan since 2012 and have significantly reduced lane change-related accidents, with a notable decrease of 24% reported in 2017. Given its effectiveness, the Driver Messenger System warrants further examination of its underlying principles and how it can be adapted for use in other countries.

To describe the movement of active particles in environments with boundaries, we use a theoretical framework. Our focus is on the behavior of active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles in environments with spherical and flat boundaries. By solving the model's equations, we find exact solutions for the particles' drift and calculate their distribution functions. Our findings show that the presence of a spherical boundary affects the particles' behavior, leading to a form of persistence that is not seen in other environments. Additionally, we examined how the particles' interaction with each other and their response time affect their distribution functions and persistence in different scenarios.

The electronic structure of complex plasmas is studied using the Siegert states expansion of the average atom model, with a focus on accurate atomic configurations. This is achieved through the computation of transition rates and cross-sections for high-charge ions, specifically hydrogen, helium, and lithium, which are then applied to a hydrogen plasma model and compared to established average atom models. The results show that the Siegert states method enhances accuracy and helps reduce the model's discrepancies, particularly when dealing with three-body processes and certain ionization channels.

The Si IV line's high-velocity flows are a common feature in solar flares, and our research aims to understand the dynamics of Si IV using AIA imaging. By comparing the redshift of Si IV to the Doppler velocity derived from AIA observations, we found a significant correlation. The difference in the observed redshift and Doppler velocity can be attributed to the motion of Si IV in relation to the observer. The transverse motion of Si IV along the line of sight can also cause discrepancies. Our results indicate that the Si IV line's redshift is primarily due to plasma flows originating from the flare's energy release region.

We present a resolution to the strong CP problem by incorporating a variable theta into the quantum chromodynamics effective Lagrangian, yet this solution is contingent upon a non-hyperbolic vacuum state. Additionally, a full solution to the strong CP problem is attainable in models where QCD belongs to a category of discrete groups, and such a solution is also present in models where the QCD gauge group is symmetric in the context of theta parameters. Furthermore, a solution to the strong CP problem is found in models where the QCD gauge group is non-Abelian and is characterized by non-hyperbolic vacuum states. Furthermore, a full solution to the strong CP problem is attainable in models where the QCD gauge group is symmetric in the context of theta parameters. Furthermore, a full solution to the strong CP problem is attainable in models where the QCD gauge group is non-Abelian and is characterised by non-hyperbolic vacuum states.

The underlying physics of ion irradiation-induced pattern formation in amorphous thin films is complex and has been the subject of various theoretical models. Despite these efforts, no consensus has been reached on a fundamental mechanism that explains the emergence of distinct patterns across different materials under similar irradiation conditions. In this research, we present a novel geometric approach that provides insight into the central problem of ion irradiation's effect on amorphous thin films. By utilizing this approach, we are able to derive the relationship between film surfaces and their underlying material structures through a geometric model. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this relationship for understanding the formation of patterns within amorphous materials subjected to ion irradiation.

This research introduces "Router", a innovative approach to source code plagiarism prevention.  By transforming original code into modified versions, Router makes it difficult for plagiarists to trace the stolen code back to its original source.  To evaluate Router's effectiveness, we conducted an experiment involving 30 participants, where they attempted to identify plagiarized code from a distorted version of the original program.  Router was compared to two control groups: one where participants accessed the original code, and another where they accessed the distorted code without Router.  The findings indicate that Router is highly effective in preventing code plagiarism detection, making it challenging for humans to trace original code from a distorted version.

This study examines the convergence properties of two classes of Dirichlet series, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_\xi$ and $\mathcal{P}_\xi^{#}$, with a focus on determining their respective convergence radii and lower bounds for absolute convergence. The research also establishes a new lower bound for the absolute convergence of series in the class $\mathcal{P}_\xi^{#}$, utilizing the concept of Bessel functions. Furthermore, the paper investigates the presence of non-convergent Dirichlet series in these classes and provides a condition for identifying such a series. An example is given to illustrate the validity of these findings.

This research explores the properties of approximately left-invariant group geometric metric spaces derived from combined $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroups and their subgroups. Specifically, it investigates the characteristics of (1) bounded metric groups in combined approximate subgroups, (2) bounded metric groups in derived from various $(k,r)$-metric approximate subgroups, (3) the existence of certain approximate subgroup structures, (4) the characteristics of a solvable Lie group with specific properties, and (4) the characteristics of a solvable Lie group with specific properties and its associated approximate subgroup structures.

This research introduces a new class of algorithms inspired by randomized and Nesterov smoothing, which enables more efficient computation of log-concave maximum likelihood estimators. Our approach is grounded in the establishment of global convergence results for smoothed Nesterov acceleration, which encompasses and extends existing convergence theories for log-concave optimization methods. Building on this foundation, we derive and analyze novel methods with guaranteed convergence, for which we establish local and global rates of convergence. A key consequence of our work is the development of a globally convergent algorithm for log-concave MLEs, coupled with explicit rates of convergence, which is underpinned by a novel smoothing technique that relies on a conditional distribution derived from the original log-likelihood function.

A simplified model of an arch formed by a collection of particles in a confined space provides valuable insights into the structural behavior of granular assemblies. By treating this arch as a rigid structure bound by mechanical constraints, researchers can gain a better understanding of its stability and how it responds to various types of disturbances. Building upon this concept, a new model for a granular column has been developed. It is found that the elements near the top and bottom of the column become highly stressed, potentially leading to the breakdown of the arch and potential jamming of the column. Furthermore, a critical threshold is identified for the column's aspect ratio, below which the column becomes unstable and a jammed state cannot be maintained.

This note introduces the $n$-bug game played on an $n$ by $n$ grid. Two players take turns placing bugs on an empty grid, with the first player winning by creating a connected path of grid squares containing exactly one bug, having visited all grid squares. We prove that the longest game duration is proportional to $n^{5/3}$ and, using a constructive proof, show optimal strategies for both $n=1$ and $n=2$.

The spectral density of random processes is a powerful tool for identifying space and time dynamics of random motion. We have investigated the spectral density of a specific type of random process, the fractional Brownian motion, and found a distinct pattern for its fractal limit. Furthermore, our research has shown that the spectral density of fractal limits is unique and can be distinguished from other types of random processes, including fractional Brownian motion and fractional stable motion, by its specific characteristics. Our results have implications for understanding the space and time dynamics of random motion and enable the identification of specific types of random processes using their spectral density.

This study demonstrates the solvability of the higher-order Broer-Kaup system through a symmetry approach. It derives the constraint condition for the constant associated with the higher-order Broer-Kaup system using symmetries. Furthermore, by introducing a convenient reduction approach, the analysis shows that the system admits a three-dimensional bijective Lie group of non-trivial symmetries in the canonical variable domain. The study also outlines the classification of the system's symmetries and explicitly presents the admitted similarity transformations.

In this study, we investigate the energy balance in nonuniform flow situations,
specifically when there's no external force and no friction. We've found that in the
absence of aligning forces, energy remains constant if two conditions are met: (i) the
vorticity does not spread; (ii) the density gradient does not change. Any external
forces that are uniform in space can be safely ignored. We've also derived a new
estimate to determine when these conditions hold, which can be applied to both
two- and three-dimensional systems. This new estimate is crucial in identifying when
these conditions hold, and it can be applied to both 2D and 3D systems. In the
instance of a rotating frame, these conditions are met if rotational averaging is
applied, which leads to the conclusion that in the absence of uniform external
forces, the energy remains constant.

We have developed a Python package for scripting the rendering process of our dataset's content, which is stored in a database. This tool enables users to generate MP4 files by selecting scenes, setting camera trajectories, and specifying rendering parameters, such as resolution and quality, using Python scripts. Although our toolkit is designed to work with the VIRUP database, it can also be used with other databases and even raw image collections, without requiring modification. We provide a few example scripts to demonstrate our toolkit's capabilities.

This paper aims to examine the Data Bricks Space Mission, an in-person and in-person like activity that is used to teach students of all ages an introduction to tabular data and data transformation concepts through an exploratory study. A survey was used to investigate the learning outcomes for participants. A total of 46 responses were analyzed, with the majority being high school students, aged between 16-18 years old. The survey revealed positive outcomes, indicating that participants perceived the activity as beneficial. The results suggest that students can grasp data joining concepts easily, and the activity is effective in engaging participants, particularly young students. However, the survey also revealed some limitations, including a need for clearer instructions and guidance, particularly for older participants, and the possibility of the activity being too easy for younger participants.

In software-defined networks, a mismatch between a network's expected data-path configuration and its actual implementation poses a significant challenge. To resolve this issue, we present a method for verifying data-path functionality in SDNs by utilizing temporal logic and model checking techniques. Our approach enables verification of data-path functionality without requiring access to a live network, instead utilizing a simulated network topology. To validate data-path behavior, we specify temporal logic rules and use them to identify any discrepancies between expected and actual data-path functionality. To enhance efficiency, we employ a hierarchical model checking technique that incorporates several optimization methods. Our approach is demonstrated through a case study involving verification of a data-path in the OpenFlow protocol.

In various fields, the ability to modify a generative model's latent code input manually is crucial. Existing techniques can achieve this, but they often require the model to be trained with supervision or specific data. We present an approach that's free from these restrictions, enabling us to alter a latent code through a simple text input. Our method assumes a limited degree of separation between the two encodings of the model: one from the data and the other from the text. By utilizing this assumption, we can implement a text-based control mechanism for a generative model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using multiple models, including DCGAN, and show that it produces coherent and visually appealing changes in the data. Furthermore, we show that it can be used to create new images by manipulating the latent code.

This research examines how the performance of the trailing foil in a two-foil arrangement is influenced by the leading foil through the interaction of the rotational wake and the leading edge vortices in a systematic study. Various parameters were altered to investigate the effect on the trailing foil, including separation points, distances between foils, speed, and the angle of attack. The investigation employed a combination of experimental and computational methods. The study found that the strength of the leading edge vortices was influenced by the separation point between the foils and that the performance of the trailing foil was enhanced when the foils were close together. The study also found that increasing speed and angle of attack led to the trailing foil experiencing a region of increased drag, but a region of lift above a critical angle of attack. The study's results were found to be consistent with the computational simulations.

The spectral function, an essential component in real-time physics, is difficult to extract from raw data due to ill-posedness, necessitating biased regularization schemes, limiting accuracy and reliability. Our approach, an ensemble learning method, boosts the confidence level of predictions, mitigating the drawbacks of prior biases, without compromising data availability. The proposed technique, rigorously evaluated within the context of the heavy-quark system using the gauge theory, achieves superior performance in both parameter estimation and prediction, outstripping the state-of-the-art in uncertainty quantification. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this novel approach and its potential for application in other fields where uncertainty quantification is crucial.

A superconducting material combined with a quantum dot creates a unique setup that can detect when electrons have passed from one end to the other, thereby identifying the addition spectrum of the superconductor. Theoretical calculations, based on the tunneling rate at different energy levels, show the spectrum's detailed structure, with notable peaks that correspond to specific electron configurations. The findings are consistent with current experimental capabilities, making it possible to examine and characterize the addition spectrum of superconducting materials like niobium with a nuclear Ginzburg-Landau parameter between 0.2 and 0.3.

The potential of generative models is being tapped into find new drug compounds by 
using them on large amounts of existing data. However, the current methods have a major 
drawback: they often produce molecules that can't be evaluated due to non-compliance 
with chemical structure rules. This limits their effectiveness in the field. We've 
developed an innovative technique that not only generates realistic molecular 
structures but also adheres to these chemical structure rules. This is achieved by 
using an unconditional generative model that is trained on two distinct types of data: 
molecular graphs and 3D molecular surface representations. This model can produce 
new molecules that accurately reflect the diversity of existing molecules while 
also being easily assessable. The 3D molecular surface representation also allows us 
to examine the potential of our generated molecules for binding with specific 
proteins, and we've successfully applied this to a case study involving COVID-19.

In their 2011 research, Accattoli and Zuccaro proposed a classification of abstract machines, which we have since adapted and expanded to include the Dynamic GoI machine (DGoIM). DGoIM functions as a go-injection engine, enabling the transfer of a term between two related types, without necessitating a beta-reduction process. Although DGoIM shares various similarities with the Lambda Calculus, it inherently resists full beta-normalisation and consequently exhibits multiple novel and distinctive reduction strategies.
